title: The number of bit strings of length that will either
subject: Theory of Computation
text: The number of bit strings of length 8 that will either start with 1 or end with 00 is?
solution: To find the number of bit strings of length 8 that either start with 1 or end with 00, we use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion. Let A be the set of strings starting with 1, and B be the set of strings ending with 00. For A, the first bit is fixed as 1, leaving 7 bits free: |A| = 2^7 = 128. For B, the last two bits are fixed as 00, leaving 6 bits free: |B| = 2^6 = 64. The intersection A ∩ B requires the first bit to be 1 and the last two bits to be 00, leaving 5 free bits: |A ∩ B| = 2^5 = 32. The total number of strings is |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B| = 128 + 64 - 32 = 160.

optionFeedback.html: This value (32) represents the intersection of both conditions (strings starting with 1 AND ending with 00). The question asks for the union of either condition.
This value (128) represents only the strings starting with 1. You must also include those ending in 00, accounting for any overlap.
Calculate the union of two sets: strings starting with 1 (2^7) and strings ending with 00 (2^6). Subtract the intersection where both conditions apply (2^5) to find the total count.
Double-counting occurs when adding cases without subtracting the intersection. Apply inclusion-exclusion to correct this.

text: Let Σ = (a,b,c,d). Then number of string in Σ4 are __________
solution:
Let Σ = {a, b, c, d}. Σ^4 denotes the set of all strings of length 4 formed from the alphabet Σ.

  • There are 4 positions in each string (length 4).

  • Each position can be filled with any of the 4 symbols from Σ.

  • Total number of strings = 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 4^4 = 256.

Answer: 256

title: How many total substrings are possible out of the string:
subject: Theory of Computation
text: How many total substrings are possible out of the string: wwxxxyyzz
solution:
Count distinct contiguous substrings of the string "wwxxxyyzz". We include the empty string in the final total.

Distinct substrings by length:

  • Length 1: {w, x, y, z} ⇒ 4

  • Length 2: {ww, wx, xx, xy, yy, yz, zz} ⇒ 7

  • Length 3: {wwx, wxx, xxx, xxy, xyy, yyz, yzz} ⇒ 7

  • Length 4: 6 distinct substrings ⇒ 6

  • Length 5: 5 distinct substrings ⇒ 5

  • Length 6: 4 distinct substrings ⇒ 4

  • Length 7: 3 distinct substrings ⇒ 3

  • Length 8: 2 distinct substrings ⇒ 2

  • Length 9: 1 substring (the whole string) ⇒ 1

Sum of non-empty distinct substrings: 4 + 7 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 39.

Including the empty string gives the final total: 39 + 1 = 40.

title: Consider the string “GATECSELECTURE” “GATECSELECTURE” is prefix of given string.
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the string “GATECSELECTURE”

S1: “GATECSELECTURE” is a prefix of given string.

S2: “GATECSELECTURE” is a suffix of given string.

S3: “CSELECTURE” is a subsequence of given string.

S4: “GTCS” is a substring of given string.

Which of the above statement is/are FALSE?
solution:
A prefix of string s is any string obtained by removing zero or more symbols from the end of s. For example, GATE, GATECSE,GATECSELECTURE and ϵ are prefixes of GATECSELECTURE.

A suffix of string s is any string obtained by removing zero or more symbols from the beginning of s. For example, LECTURE, CSELECTURE,GATECSELECTURE and ϵ are suffixes of GATECSELECTURE.

Evaluation of each statement:

  • S1 — "GATECSELECTURE is a prefix": True. The given string equals "GATECSELECTURE", and a string is a prefix of itself.

  • S2 — "GATECSELECTURE is a suffix": True. For the same reason as S1, the whole string is also a suffix of itself.

  • S3 — "CSELECTURE is a subsequence": True. Those characters appear in order and in fact contiguously at positions 5–14, so it is a subsequence (and a substring).

  • S4 — "GTCS is a substring": False. While the letters G, T, C, S appear in that order as a subsequence (positions 1, 3, 5, 6), they do not appear contiguously, so "GTCS" is not a substring.

Conclusion: Only the statement that "GTCS is a substring" is false. Therefore the correct answer is the choice that says only S4 is false.

optionFeedback.html: This choice claims that only the statements "GATECSELECTURE is a prefix" and "GATECSELECTURE is a suffix" are false. That is incorrect. Both statements are true because the string equals "GATECSELECTURE" exactly, and any string is both a prefix and a suffix of itself. Therefore this choice is wrong.

Correct. The statements that the entire string is a prefix and a suffix are true (a string is a prefix and suffix of itself). "CSELECTURE" is also true because those characters appear contiguously (positions 5–14), so it is a subsequence (in fact a substring). "GTCS" is false as a substring because those four characters do not occur contiguously in that order; they only occur as a subsequence (positions 1,3,5,6).

This choice claims that "CSELECTURE" and "GTCS" are false. That is incorrect. "CSELECTURE" is true because those characters appear in order and contiguously (positions 5–14), so it is a subsequence (and a substring). "GTCS" is indeed false as a substring, but because "CSELECTURE" is true this choice is incorrect.

This choice claims that only "CSELECTURE" is false. That is incorrect because "CSELECTURE" is actually present in the string (positions 5–14), so it is true. The false statement is "GTCS" being a substring, not "CSELECTURE".

title: Let {ab, aa, baa}. Which of the following strings are
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Let L = {ab, aa, baa}. Which of the following strings are not in L*.
solution:
Solution: We check each given string for membership in L*, where L = {ab, aa, baa}.

  • abaabaaabaa: This string is in L*. One valid decomposition is ab · aa · baa · ab · aa.

  • aaaabaaaa: This string is in L*. A valid decomposition is aa · aa · baa · aa.

  • baaaaabaaaab: This string is not in L*. Proof by parsing from the end:

    1. Only the word 'ab' ends with the letter 'b', so the final two letters 'ab' must form the last token. Remove that 'ab'.

    2. The remaining suffix now ends with 'aa', so the preceding token must be 'aa' (the three-letter word 'baa' would require the last three letters to be 'baa', which they are not). Remove that 'aa'.

    3. After these removals the remaining prefix ends with 'ba' and its last three letters are 'aba'. Neither 'aa' nor 'baa' matches these ending letters, so no valid final token exists for the prefix. This contradiction means no full decomposition into words from L is possible.

  • baaaaabaa: This string is in L*. One valid decomposition is baa · aa · ab · aa.

Conclusion: Among the four given strings, only baaaaabaaaab cannot be written as a concatenation of words from L, so it is not in L*.

optionFeedback.html: abaabaaabaa is in L*. One valid decomposition is ab · aa · baa · ab · aa, which uses only the words 'ab', 'aa', and 'baa' from L.
aaaabaaaa is in L*. A valid decomposition is aa · aa · baa · aa, which uses only words from L.

baaaaabaaaab is not in L*. Reason: only 'ab' ends with b, so the final 'ab' must be a token; removing it leaves a prefix whose last two letters are 'aa', so the previous token would have to be 'aa' (since the three-letter word 'baa' would require the last three letters to be 'baa', which they are not). Removing that 'aa' leaves a prefix whose last two letters are 'ba' and last three letters are 'aba', so it cannot end with 'aa' or 'baa'. This contradiction shows no decomposition into words from L is possible, so the string is not in L*.
baaaaabaa is in L*. One valid decomposition is baa · aa · ab · aa, which uses only the words 'baa', 'aa', and 'ab' from L.

This is the tally a student gets by mistakenly treating q3 as an accepting state alongside q4 — q3 only self-loops on '0' and forwards to q4 on '1', but is never itself an accepting state, so crediting it as accepting counts strings that merely stop there as if they too belonged to the accepted set.

title: The number of states required by Finite State Machine, to
subject: Theory of Computation
text: The number of states required by a Finite State Machine, to simulate the behavior of a computer with a memory capable of storing 'm' words, each of length 'n' bits is?
solution:
The total memory capacity is determined by the number of words multiplied by the length of each word.

Total bits = m × n.

Each bit can be in one of two states (0 or 1). Therefore, the total number of unique memory configurations is 2 raised to the power of the total bits.

Thus, the number of states required is 2^(mn).

optionFeedback.html: This option does not correctly represent the state space required for all possible memory configurations.
This option suggests an additive relationship between parameters, but state space depends on total bit capacity.
The number of states depends on the total number of unique memory configurations. Since every bit can be 0 or 1, the state space expands exponentially with total bits rather than linearly.
The number of states depends on total bit combinations, which grows exponentially with the memory size, not by adding words and lengths.

title: Let na(w) mod or na(w) mod where na(w) is the
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Q. Let L={ w ∣ na(w) mod 13 = 1 or na(w) mod 15 = 5 }, where na(w) is the number of letter a in string w.

What is the number of accepting states in a minimal DFA that keeps track of na(w) modulo the necessary value(s)? (MCQ)
solution:
We must track the number of a's modulo both 13 and 15. The natural way is to track residues modulo lcm(13,15) = 195 so we can test both congruences simultaneously.

  • Residues satisfying na(w) ≡ 1 (mod 13): there are 195/13 = 15 such residues modulo 195.

  • Residues satisfying na(w) ≡ 5 (mod 15): there are 195/15 = 13 such residues modulo 195.

  • Intersection (both congruences): by the Chinese Remainder Theorem there is exactly 1 residue modulo 195 satisfying both na(w) ≡ 1 (mod 13) and na(w) ≡ 5 (mod 15).

  • Using inclusion–exclusion, the number of accepting residues is 15 + 13 − 1 = 27.

Answer: 27 accepting states.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Counting residues modulo 13 alone gives one residue per 13, but the DFA must track counts modulo the least common multiple 195 to account for both conditions. There are 15 residues modulo 195 that satisfy the congruence na(w) ≡ 1 (mod 13), so 13 is not the correct number of accepting states.

Incorrect. This is close but off by one. When tracking residues modulo 195, there are 15 residues satisfying na(w) ≡ 1 (mod 13) and 13 residues satisfying na(w) ≡ 5 (mod 15). Using inclusion–exclusion gives 15 + 13 − 1 = 27 accepting residues, not 26.

Correct. Track na(w) modulo lcm(13,15)=195. There are 195/13 = 15 residues with na(w) ≡ 1 (mod 13) and 195/15 = 13 residues with na(w) ≡ 5 (mod 15). Their intersection is a single residue by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, so the union size is 15 + 13 − 1 = 27 accepting residues.

Incorrect. 195 is the total number of states when tracking na(w) modulo 195, but only some of those are accepting. Only residues that meet either congruence are accepting; using inclusion–exclusion yields 27 accepting residues out of 195.

title: The FSM (Finite State Machine) machine pictured in the figure
subject: Theory of Computation
text: The FSM (Finite State Machine) machine pictured in the figure above

options.html: Finds 2's complement of a given bit pattern

solution:
Read the input string least-significant-bit (LSB) first and treat the two right-hand states as a serial 'add 1' (increment) circuit, where one path means a carry is still pending and the other means the carry has already been absorbed.

Starting in the initial state we are adding 1, so a carry is pending. On the first input bit 0 the machine outputs 1 (0+1 = 1, carry resolved) and moves to the carry-absorbed (copy) state; on the first input bit 1 it outputs 0 (1+1 = 10, write 0, carry out) and stays on the carry-pending path.

On the carry-pending path each further input 1 outputs 0 and keeps the carry (a run of trailing 1s all become 0); the first input 0 outputs 1 and the carry is absorbed, after which every remaining bit is copied through unchanged.

Worked example (LSB first): input 0,1,1 represents 110 = 6. The machine emits 1,1,1 which reads back as 111 = 7 = 6 + 1. Input 1,1,1 = 7 emits 0,0,0 = 0, i.e. 7 + 1 with overflow. In every case the output equals the input increased by one.

Therefore the finite state machine increments the given bit pattern by 1.

optionFeedback.html: A pure complementer must flip every bit independently. Trace this Mealy machine on a string fed least-significant-bit first: once it leaves the carry path it copies the remaining bits unchanged rather than inverting them, so it is not a bit-wise complementer.

The 2's-complement rule (scan from the LSB, copy bits up to and including the first 1, then invert the rest) is not what these transitions produce. Trace the machine LSB-first and compare the output with the true 2's complement; they differ, so this is not the operation performed.

Trace the machine least-significant-bit first, viewing the two right-hand paths as a carry that is still pending versus a carry already absorbed. Follow several example strings through the transitions and write down the output before committing to any single interpretation of what the machine does.

Changing only the sign bit would alter a single fixed bit position and leave every other bit untouched. This machine transforms a contiguous run of bits starting from the least-significant end, not one isolated sign position, so this description does not match its behaviour.

text: Determine the language recognized by the following DFA?

options.html: Strings containing exactly two 0's and exactly two 1's
Strings containing at least two 0's and at least two 1's

solution:
Answer: Strings containing at least two 0's and at least two 1's.

Key idea: The DFA has nine states that track, independently for 0 and 1, whether the count seen so far is 0, 1, or at least 2. The accepting state represents both counts being at least two.

  • Start state corresponds to seeing 0 zeros and 0 ones.

  • Transitions on 0 or 1 move you to states that increase the corresponding count, with each count saturating at the "at least 2" level.

  • The sole accepting state is reached only after both counts are in the "at least 2" category; that state loops on both 0 and 1 so any additional symbols are allowed.

  • Therefore the language is all binary strings that contain at least two 0's and at least two 1's.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. This DFA does not enforce parity. Consider the following languages:

Minimum number of states in DFA for the above languages:

Answer: The true statements are the second and the third (L2 and L3 only).

  • L1: L1 = { a^{m^n} | n ≥ 1, m ≥ n } is not regular. It requires comparing unbounded exponent relationships (similar in difficulty to languages that force unbounded numeric relationships), so there is no finite-state DFA that recognizes it. Hence the claim that it needs four states is false.

This equality of unbounded substrings is analogous to the non-regular language {ww}, so L4 is not regular and cannot be recognized by any finite-state DFA (in particular not by a four-state DFA).

title: Minimum number of states in DFA for given language:
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Minimum number of states in DFA for given language:
solution:
Key idea: use Myhill–Nerode (right-invariant residuals) to count distinct states.

Describe the language:

  • L = {a^n | n = 3 or n = 2m for some m ≥ 1}.

  • Accepted lengths: 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, ... (all even ≥ 2, plus 3).

Compute residuals R_i = {k ≥ 0 | i + k ∈ L} for small i (these correspond to different states if they differ):

  • R0 = {k | k ∈ L} = {2,3,4,6,8,...}.

  • R1 = {k | 1 + k ∈ L} = {1,2,3,5,7,9,...}.

  • R2 = {k | 2 + k ∈ L} = {0,1,2,4,6,8,...}.

  • R3 = {k | 3 + k ∈ L} = {0} ∪ {odd k ≥ 1} = {0,1,3,5,7,...}.

For any i ≥ 4 the future behavior is periodic of period 2 (depends only on parity):

  • If i ≥ 4 is even then Ri = {k | k is even} (since i + k ≥ 4 and acceptance is just parity even).

  • If i ≥ 5 is odd then Ri = {k | k is odd}.

These six residuals are all distinct:

  1. R0 (distinct because it does not contain 0 or 1 but contains 2 and 3).

  2. R1 (distinct because 0 ∉ R1 but 1 ∈ R1).

  3. R2 (contains 0,1,2 and even numbers ≥4) — different from the generic even class because it contains 1.

  4. R3 (contains 0 and all odd k ≥1) — different from the generic odd class because it contains 0.

  5. The generic even class for i ≥ 4 (Ri = even k) is different from R2 because R2 contains 1.

  6. The generic odd class for i ≥ 5 (Ri = odd k) is different from R3 because R3 contains 0.

Thus there are exactly six distinct equivalence classes, so any minimal DFA must have 6 states.

Which of those states are accepting? Precisely the classes Ri that contain 0, i.e. the classes corresponding to lengths that themselves belong to L: R2, R3, and the generic even class (i even ≥ 4).

Conclusion: minimal DFA requires 6 states (matches the given answer).

title: Can DFA recognize palindrome number? DFA (palindrome number)
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Can a DFA recognize a palindrome number?
solution:
A Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) has a finite number of states and no external memory. To recognize a palindrome, the machine must compare the first half of the input string with the reversed second half. This requires remembering an unbounded number of symbols, which a DFA cannot do.

Therefore, a DFA cannot recognize the language of palindromes. A Pushdown Automaton (PDA), which includes a stack for memory, is required for this task.

एक निर्धारित परिमित ऑटोमेटन (DFA) की केवल परिमित संख्या में अवस्थाएं होती हैं और इसमें कोई बाहरी मेमोरी नहीं होती है। एक पैलिंड्रोम को पहचानने के लिए, मशीन को इनपुट स्ट्रिंग के पहले आधे हिस्से को दूसरे आधे हिस्से के उल्टे के साथ तुलना करनी होगी। इसके लिए अनंत संख्या में प्रतीकों को याद रखने की आवश्यकता होती है, जिसे एक DFA नहीं कर सकता।

Finite automata cannot count or remember an unbounded number of symbols to verify symmetry. Palindrome recognition requires a stack or infinite memory, which exceeds the capabilities of a DFA, making this the correct choice.

The limitation of DFAs regarding palindromes is a well-established theoretical fact. It is definitively impossible for a DFA to recognize the language of all palindromes over any alphabet.

A DFA is minimal when every state is reachable and every pair of distinct states is distinguishable by some suffix: processing that suffix from the two states produces different acceptance results.

For a DFA graph, the recognized language is found by tracing transitions from the start state to accepting or non-accepting states.

The correct option is C (Only S3).

For example, an NFA with 10 poorly optimized states might recognize a language that a minimal DFA can recognize in just 2 states. (The most fundamental relationship taught in automata theory is the upper bound. If a given NFA has N states, the equivalent DFA can have a maximum of 2^N states.)

  • S3 is TRUE: As explained above, an NFA and its corresponding DFA can have the exact same number of states (specifically, when the NFA requires no subset construction expansion and is already deterministic in nature).

title: Consider the following definition of machine such that set of
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the following definition of machine (M) such that

Q: set of states

Σ: alphabet

Q0 : is start state

F ⊆ Q is set of final states

δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → Q

M represents
solution:
Concept:

The standard automaton classes differ in the DOMAIN and CODOMAIN of their transition function δ:

  • Deterministic finite automaton (DFA): δ: Q × Σ → Q — every input symbol comes from Σ only (no ε in the domain), and the output is exactly one next state.

  • Non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA), plain form: δ: Q × Σ → 2Q — no ε in the domain, and the output is a SET of possible next states, i.e. an element of the power set of Q, not a single state.

  • ε-NFA (NFA extended with ε-transitions): δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → 2Q — ε is additionally allowed in the domain, but the codomain is still the power set 2Q, never a single state.

  • Pushdown automaton (PDA): the transition function also takes a stack symbol as input and returns state–stack-string pairs, i.e. δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ → 2(Q×Γ*).

Application:

Machine M's transition function is δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → Q. Check it against each signature above:

  1. Domain check: M's δ accepts ε as an input, alongside Σ. A standard DFA's δ never takes ε as input, so M cannot be a DFA on this ground alone.

  2. Codomain check: M's δ maps to Q — a single state — not to 2Q (the power set of Q). Both the plain-NFA and ε-NFA definitions require the codomain 2Q in every case, so M's single-state output rules out NFA and ε-NFA alike, regardless of what its domain contains.

  3. Stack check: M's tuple (Q, Σ, Q0, F, δ) has no stack alphabet Γ, and δ produces no stack operation, so M also cannot be a PDA.

Cross-check:

M keeps the ε-input feature associated with an ε-NFA but keeps the single-next-state output associated with a DFA — a combination that matches neither formal signature (and, having no stack, does not match PDA either).

A function that maps to a single state can always be re-encoded, after the fact, as a restricted (singleton-valued) case of a broader relation or power-set-valued map — but that re-encoding is a DIFFERENT mathematical object from the one M's definition actually states. Classifying M means matching its STATED signature δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → Q exactly against the DFA/NFA/ε-NFA/PDA definitions above, not asking whether some reformulation of it could be embedded inside a larger class; by that looser standard every DFA could equally be called an NFA, which would erase the very distinction this definition is testing.

So M's transition function, taken as stated, does not correspond to the standard DFA, NFA, ε-NFA, or PDA definitions.

Result: M represents "None of the above."

optionFeedback.html: A standard deterministic finite automaton's transition function has the signature δ: Q × Σ → Q — every input symbol comes strictly from the alphabet Σ, with no ε argument in the domain.

A standard non-deterministic finite automaton's transition function has the signature δ: Q × Σ → 2Q — its domain is restricted to Σ alone (no ε), and its output is a set of possible next states (an element of the power set of Q), not a single state.
A standard pushdown automaton's transition function additionally takes a stack symbol as input and returns state–stack-string pairs, giving it the signature δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ → 2(Q×Γ*).

This choice applies whenever a machine's stated transition-function signature — its domain and codomain together — does not coincide with the standard deterministic finite automaton, non-deterministic finite automaton, or pushdown automaton signatures.

title: Which of the following is/are not regular?
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following is/are not regular?
solution:
Final answer: the non-regular languages are the sets of the form { ω (ω^R)^+ | ω ∈ (a+b)(a+b)^+ } and { w w | w ∈ (a+b)^+ }.

Explanations and proof sketches:

  • Language: { ω (ω^R)^+ | ω ∈ (a+b)(a+b)^+ } — not regular.

    Reason (pumping-lemma sketch): this language contains the subset { w w^R | w ∈ (a+b)^+ } (take one copy of ω^R). The set of strings formed by a word followed by its reverse is a standard non-regular language. Let p be the pumping length. Choose w = a^p b and let s = w w^R = a^p b b a^p. Any decomposition s = xyz with |xy| ≤ p forces y to lie inside the initial a^p. Pumping changes the number of a's in the left half but not in the right half, so the pumped string cannot be of the form u u^R. This contradicts the pumping lemma, so the language is not regular.

  • Language: { w w | w ∈ (a+b)^+ } — not regular.

    Reason (classic pumping-lemma): assume regular with pumping length p. Let w = a^p b and take s = w w = a^p b a^p b. Any split xyz with |xy| ≤ p places y inside the first a^p. Pumping down removes some a's from the first half but leaves the second half unchanged, so the pumped string cannot remain of the form u u. This contradiction shows the language is not regular.

  • Language: { ω^n ω^m | n,m ≥ 1 } with ω ranging over (a+b)* — regular.

    Reason: for any fixed nonempty ω we have ω^n ω^m = ω^{n+m}, so the set for that ω is ω^+. Taking the union over all nonempty ω yields every nonempty string (each nonempty string x appears as x^1). Hence the union equals (a+b)^+, which is regular. (If ω were allowed to be the empty string, that contributes only the empty string; the union over nonempty ω still gives (a+b)^+.)

  • Language: { ω (ω^R)* | ω ∈ (a+b)(a+b)^+ } — regular.

    Reason: (ω^R)* includes the empty string, so for each allowed ω the word ω itself is in the set (take zero repeats). Because ω ranges over all strings of length at least two, every string of length ≥2 appears (choose ω to be that string). Therefore the union contains all strings of length at least two, i.e. the language equals the regular set of all strings of length ≥2. Thus it is regular.

Summary: Non-regular — the languages that force exact mirroring or exact duplication (the ω(ω^R)^+ family contains w w^R and the ww family). Regular — the other two languages, since one simplifies to (a+b)^+ and the other equals the set of all strings of length ≥2.

optionFeedback.html: Language: { ω (ω^R)^+ | ω ∈ (a+b)(a+b)^+ }. This is not regular. Reason (sketch): it contains the subset { w w^R | w ∈ (a+b)^+ } (take one copy of ω^R). The set { w w^R } (even-length palindromes built as w followed by reverse(w)) is not regular. Use the pumping-lemma: choose pumping length p and the string s = a^p b b a^p (with w = a^p b). Any decomposition with |xy| ≤ p forces y inside the first a^p block; pumping changes the left block’s number of a’s but leaves the right block unchanged, so the pumped string cannot be of the form w w^R. Thus the language is not regular.

title: Consider the following languages: Which of the following is Regular?
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Consider the following languages: Which of the following is Regular?
solution:
Answer: None of L1, L2, L3 is regular.

Key fact: A language over a unary alphabet {a} is regular iff the set of exponents is ultimately periodic (there exist integers p > 0 and N such that for all n ≥ N, membership of n depends only on n mod p).

  • L1 = { a^n | n is not a prime number }: Not regular.

    Reason: If the set of non-prime lengths were regular then its complement (the set of primes) would be regular as well (regular languages are closed under complement). Any regular unary set is ultimately periodic; but the primes cannot be ultimately periodic. Indeed, assuming primes are ultimately periodic with period p and threshold N, any residue class r (mod p) that contains a prime > N would then have all sufficiently large numbers congruent to r be prime. Choose a prime q not dividing p and large enough; the congruence kp ≡ -r (mod q) has a solution k, giving a number r + kp divisible by q and larger than q, hence composite — contradiction. Thus primes are not regular, so L1 is not regular.

  • L2 = { a^n | n = k^3 for some k ≥ 0 }: Not regular.

    Reason: Consecutive cubes differ by (k+1)^3 - k^3 = 3k^2 + 3k + 1, which grows without bound. If the set of cube exponents were ultimately periodic with period p then for large k the gap between consecutive cube exponents would be ≤ p, contradicting the unbounded gap. Therefore the set of cubes is not ultimately periodic, so L2 is not regular.

  • L3 = { a^n | n = 2^k for some k ≥ 0 }: Not regular.

    Reason: Consecutive powers of two differ by 2^{k+1} - 2^k = 2^k, which grows without bound. By the same ultimately-periodic criterion, this unbounded gap prevents a fixed period p from describing membership beyond some threshold. Hence L3 is not regular.

Conclusion: None of L1, L2, L3 is regular.

L1 (all non-prime lengths) is not regular because if its complement (the primes) were regular then primes would be eventually periodic, which leads to a contradiction (one can show a residue class mod any putative period must contain composite numbers). L2 (perfect cubes) is not regular because in unary a regular language must be ultimately periodic, but gaps between consecutive cubes grow without bound (so no fixed period can describe membership beyond some point).

This choice lists L1 only. L1 is not regular. If the set of non-prime lengths were regular then its complement (the primes) would be regular too, but the set of primes in unary cannot be ultimately periodic: assuming a period leads to a residue class forced to contain only primes beyond some point, yet one can find composite numbers in that residue class, a contradiction. Thus L1 is non-regular.

This choice lists L2 and L3. Neither is regular. For L2 (cubes): consecutive cubes differ by 3k^2+3k+1, which tends to infinity, so there is no fixed period that would make membership ultimately periodic. For L3 (powers of two): consecutive powers differ by 2^k, which also grows without bound, so membership cannot be ultimately periodic. Since unary regular languages must be ultimately periodic, both languages are non-regular.

This choice states that none of L1, L2, L3 is regular. Correct. Summary: regular unary languages are exactly those whose set of exponents is ultimately periodic. L2 (cubes) and L3 (powers of two) have unbounded gaps between consecutive exponents, so they are not ultimately periodic. L1 would imply the primes (its complement) are regular; primes are not ultimately periodic by a residue-class contradiction argument, so L1 is not regular. Therefore none of the three is regular.

The language is every binary string that contains at least two 1's, with the 1's allowed anywhere and any number of 0's in between, before, or after.

title: The given finite automata is equivalent to which of the
subject: Theory of Computation
text: The given finite automaton is equivalent to which of the following regular expressions?
solution:
Concept: A finite automaton accepts exactly those strings that can be spelled out along some path from the start state to an accepting state. Turning such a diagram into a regular expression rests on three correspondences: consecutive edges along one path become concatenation, alternative routes become a union (+), and a self-loop that carries every alphabet symbol becomes (a + b)*. When a state has two edges on the same symbol the machine is non-deterministic, so a string is accepted as soon as one route works, and the whole language is the union taken over all start-to-accepting routes.

Application: In this diagram the start state q0 branches on a to q1 and to q4, and on b to q5; the state q2 carries a self-loop labelled a, b; and qf is the only accepting state. Every route from q0 to qf therefore has one of three shapes.

  1. q0 —a→ q1 —b→ qf spells the string ab.

  2. q0 —a→ q4 —a→ q2, then the a, b self-loop on q2 any number of times, then q2 —b→ qf spells aa (a + b)* b.

  3. q0 —b→ q5 —b→ q2, then the same self-loop, then q2 —b→ qf spells bb (a + b)* b.

Taking the union of the three shapes and factoring out the shared (a + b)* b tail gives ab + aa (a + b)* b + bb (a + b)* b = ab + (aa + bb) (a + b)* b.

Cross-check: Test the result against the diagram on concrete strings: ab is accepted; aab is accepted through q0, q4, q2, qf; aaab is accepted by looping once on q2; baa is rejected because q5 has no edge on a; and no accepted string of length two or more ends in a, because every edge entering qf carries the label b.

Contrast with the other patterns:

  • (a + b)* (aa + bb) (a + b)* denotes every string that contains aa or bb somewhere, so it takes in aa and baa, which the diagram does not accept.

  • ab (aa + bb) (a + b)* b forces the two symbols ab in front of the double letter, so it leaves out aab and aaab, which the diagram does accept.

  • ab (aa + b) (a + b)* a ends every string it denotes with a, while every edge entering qf carries the label b.

The regular expression equivalent to the given finite automaton is therefore ab + (aa + bb) (a + b)* b.

optionFeedback.html: This pattern is a concatenation: every string it denotes carries an unrestricted block of a and b symbols on each side of aa or bb, so it contains aa or bb somewhere and has no restriction on the first or the last symbol. Strings it denotes include aa, bb, baa and abba.

This pattern is a union: the two-symbol string ab, together with every string whose first two symbols are aa or bb and whose last symbol is b, with anything in between. Strings it denotes include ab, aab, bbb and aabab.

This pattern is a concatenation: every string it denotes starts with ab, continues with aa or bb, and ends with b, with anything in between. Strings it denotes include abaab, abbbb, abaabb and abbbab.

This pattern is a concatenation: every string it denotes starts with ab, continues with aa or a single b, and ends with a, with anything in between. Strings it denotes include abba, abaaa, abaaba and abbaa.

title: Which grammar type generates context-free languages
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which grammar type generates context-free languages ?
solution: Chomsky's hierarchy classifies formal grammars into four types based on their production rules and the languages they generate. Type 2 grammars, also known as Context-Free Grammars (CFGs), are specifically defined by their ability to generate context-free languages. In a Type 2 grammar, every production rule has exactly one non-terminal symbol on the left-hand side and any string of terminals and/or non-terminals on the right-hand side. This structure allows the replacement of a variable to occur independently of its surrounding context, which is the defining characteristic of context-free languages.Type 0 grammars (Option A) generate recursively enumerable languages and have no restrictions on their production rules. Type 1 grammars (Option B) generate context-sensitive languages, where the length of the right-hand side must be greater than or equal to the left-hand side. title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 35

text: Any syntactic construct that can be described by a regular expression can also be described by a:
solution:
Concept: The Chomsky hierarchy classifies grammars by the generative power of their production rules. Type-3 (regular) grammars are the most restricted, permitting only productions of the form A -> aB or A -> a. Type-2 (context-free) grammars are strictly more general: they permit any production A -> alpha with a single non-terminal on the left-hand side and any string alpha of terminals/non-terminals on the right. Because every type in the hierarchy is nested inside the ones above it, any language generated by a lower type is also generated by every higher type.

  1. A regular expression denotes a regular language, and by Kleene's theorem this is exactly the class of languages accepted by a finite automaton.

  2. Every regular language has an equivalent right-linear (Type-3) grammar, whose productions are restricted to the form A -> aB or A -> a.

  3. A context-free (Type-2) grammar allows any production A -> alpha with one non-terminal on the left; the restricted right-linear form is already a special case of this, so no production needs to be rewritten.

  4. Consequently, the same language generated by the right-linear grammar is simultaneously a valid context-free-grammar derivation, so any syntactic construct describable by a regular expression is also describable by a context-free grammar.

Cross-check: this containment also follows from automata equivalence -- a pushdown automaton that never uses its stack behaves exactly like a finite automaton, and every pushdown automaton has an equivalent context-free grammar, so the finite-automaton language is a CFG language too. The reverse containment fails: the language {an bn | n >= 0} is context-free but has no equivalent regular expression, confirming that context-free grammars are a strict superset of regular languages rather than the reverse.

Result: the correct classification is Context free grammar.

Note: because Type-1 (context-sensitive) and Type-0 (unrestricted) grammars also contain every context-free language, a broader class such as context-sensitive grammar is technically also capable of describing the same construct; standard exam convention for grammar-hierarchy classification questions scores the tightest, most specific sufficient class among those offered, which is the context-free grammar.

title: Consider the following grammar: ABSc Abc BA AB Bb bb
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the following grammar:

S → ABSc | Abc

BA → AB

Bb → bb

Ab → ab

Aa → aa

The language generated by the above grammar is the set of all strings made up of a, b, c such that

options.html: The number of a's, b's, and c's will be equal but the order of occurrence is not fixed
The number of a's is twice the number of b's and equal to that of c's
The number of a's is equal to the number of b's and b's always precede c's
The number of a's, b's, and c's are the same and the a's precede b's, which precede c's

solution:
Language described: { a^n b^n c^n | n ≥ 1 } — equal numbers of a's, b's, and c's in the order a then b then c.

  • Use S -> ABSc repeatedly (n−1 times), then apply S -> Abc once to obtain a sentential form with n occurrences of A, n occurrences of B, and n occurrences of c: A^n B^n c^n (with A and B still nonterminals).

  • Use BA -> AB to move every A to the left of all B's, so the A's form a contiguous block before the B's.

  • Convert nonterminals into terminals using the rules Bb -> bb, Ab -> ab, and Aa -> aa. These rules progressively change B's and A's into b's and a's while preserving counts.

  • Thus every derivation yields a string a^n b^n c^n, and every string of that form can be generated by choosing the appropriate number of S -> ABSc applications.

  • Worked example (n=2):

  • S => ABSc => AB Abc => A B A b c c

  • Apply BA -> AB: A B A b c c => A A B b c c

  • Apply Bb -> bb: A A B b c c => A A b b c c

  • Convert A's: Ab -> ab then Aa -> aa to get a a b b c c.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The grammar does not allow the letters to appear in arbitrary order. It enforces that all a's come before all b's and all b's come before all c's, and it produces equal numbers of a, b, and c, so the order is fixed as a...b...c....
Incorrect. The grammar does not make the number of a's twice the number of b's. Instead it enforces that the counts of a, b, and c are equal.

Incorrect/Incomplete. It is true that b's precede c's, but the grammar also requires that a's precede b's. The full restriction is that the string consists of a block of a's, then a block of b's, then a block of c's, with equal numbers of each.

Correct. The grammar generates exactly the language { a^n b^n c^n | n ≥ 1 }: equal numbers of a's, b's, and c's with all a's before all b's before all c's. Brief derivation idea: apply S -> ABSc (n-1) times then S -> Abc to obtain A^n B^n c^n; use BA -> AB to move A's left, then Bb -> bb, Ab -> ab, Aa -> aa to convert nonterminals to terminals. Example for n=2: S => ABSc => ABAbc => A B A b c c => BA -> AB gives A A B b c c => Bb -> bb gives A A b b c c => Ab -> ab and Aa -> aa give a a b b c c.

Which of the regular expressions corresponds to this grammar?

solution:
This type of grammar generates a set of strings where a sequence from L(A) is followed by a sequence from L(B), and the overall structure S→AS allows for repetition of L(A).

The given grammar is:

  1. S→AB∣AS

  2. A→a∣aA

  3. B→b

1. Language for A (L(A))

The rules for A are:

A→a∣aA

  • A→a is the base case (generates a single 'a').

  • A→aA allows one or more 'a's to be prepended. The strings generated by A are {a,aa,aaa,…}. The corresponding regular expression is a+, which is equivalent to aa∗.

2. Language for B (L(B))

The rule for B is simple:

B→b

The language generated by B is {b}. The regular expression is b.

3. Language for S (L(S))

The rules for S are:

S→AB∣AS

The set of strings generated by this structure is (L(A))+L(B).

  • S→AB: This generates the base case: one sequence from L(A) followed by L(B). This is a+b.

  • S→AS: This is the recursive rule. It allows a string from L(A) to be placed before any string generated by S. This ensures that at least one L(A) occurs, followed by the main L(A)L(B) part. However, in this specific structure, S always terminates with B, and the A's pile up before the B.

Let's trace a few derivations:

  • S→AB →(a)(b)=ab

  • S→AS →aS→aAB→a(a)(b)=aab

  • S→AS →aS→aAS→aaAB→aa(a)(b)=aaab

The generated strings are {ab,aab,aaab,…}. This is the language of one or more 'a's followed by exactly one 'b'. The regular expression is a+b, which is one of the standard forms for aa∗b.

title: Consider the following grammar with the following productions: xAy yAx
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the grammar G with productions:

S -> xAy | yAx
A -> xAy | yAx | xAx | yAy | epsilon

Let T be the total number of states and F be the number of final states in the minimum DFA for the language generated by G. Find the value of T - F.
solution:
Correct answer: 5.

The nonterminal A can generate any even-length string over {x, y}: each production adds one symbol on the left and one symbol on the right, and the symbols are chosen independently.

Then S -> xAy | yAx forces the generated string to have even length, length at least 2, and different first and last symbols. So the language is:

L = { w over {x, y} | |w| is even, |w| > 0, and the first and last symbols of w are different }.

For the minimum DFA, we need:
1 start state before reading the first symbol;
2 odd-length states, depending on whether the first symbol was x or y;
4 even-length states, depending on the first symbol (x/y) and current last symbol (x/y).

Thus total states T = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

The final states are the two even-length cases where first and last symbols are different: first x and last y, or first y and last x. Hence F = 2.

Therefore T - F = 7 - 2 = 5.

Answer: 2 incorrect statements. The claims "Every subset of a regular language is regular" and "Every subset of an infinite language is regular" are false; the claim about finite languages is true.

Reasoning and examples:

  • The claim "Every subset of an infinite language is regular" is false. Counterexample: an infinite regular language such as Σ* contains non-regular subsets (for example {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0}), so an infinite language can have non-regular subsets.

solution:
Answer: The statement "Infinite union of regular languages may be regular." is true.

  • Why it is true: "may be regular" means sometimes the infinite union is regular. Example: the infinite union ⋃_{k≥0}{a^k} = {a^n | n≥0} = a*, which is regular.

  • Why the property is not universal: an infinite union of regular languages can be non-regular. Example: for each n let R_n = {a^n b^n} (each R_n is finite and therefore regular); the union ⋃_{n≥0} R_n = {a^n b^n | n≥0} is not regular.

  • Statement: "Complement of every subset of regular languages is regular."

text:

solution:
Key idea: for any language L over the alphabet Σ, L ∪ complement(L) = Σ* (the universal language).

  • Apply the identity to the inner union: L2 ∪ complement(L2) = Σ*.

  • Then the full expression L1 ∪ (L2 ∪ complement(L2)) becomes L1 ∪ Σ* = Σ*.

  • Σ* is regular, so that language is always regular regardless of facts about L1 and L2.

Therefore the expression that is always regular is the one of the form L1 ∪ (L2 ∪ complement(L2)).

Notes on the other expressions:

  • For the expression L1 ∩ complement(L2): this equals L1 \ L2. Although every DCFL is recursive (decidable), that does not imply every string of L1 belongs to L2. The difference L1 \ L2 can be empty, finite, regular, or non-regular depending on the choices of L1 and L2. For example, if L1 is a non-regular DCFL like {a^n b^n} and L2 is chosen to exclude those strings, then the intersection equals that non-regular DCFL. Thus regularity is not guaranteed.

  • For the expression complement(L1) ∪ complement(L2): by De Morgan this is complement(L1 ∩ L2). There is no general reason this must be regular. It can be Σ* in some cases (e.g., if L1 = ∅) or non-regular in others (e.g., if L1 = Σ* and L2 is a non-regular RE language, then complement(L1 ∩ L2) = complement(L2) need not be regular).

title: Given that is language accepted by finite state machine, which
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Given that L is a language accepted by a finite state machine, which of the following is also accepted by some finite state machine?

options.html: LR = {S ∣ S is obtained by reversing all strings in L)

solution:
Answer: All four languages are regular.

  • Prefixes (Prefix(L)): Given a DFA for L, mark every state that can reach some final state as accepting. The resulting DFA accepts exactly the prefixes of strings in L.

  • Reverse (reverse(L)): Regular languages are closed under reversal. Reverse all transitions of an automaton for L and swap start and final states (or build an NFA with epsilon-transitions from a new start to the old finals); the new NFA accepts the reversed strings.

  • Complement ({0,1}* − L): Over the alphabet {0,1}, regular languages are closed under complement. Make a complete DFA for L (add a dead state if needed) and then swap accepting and non-accepting states to obtain a DFA for the complement.

  • Kleene star (L*): Regular languages are closed under Kleene star. From an NFA for L, add a new start state that is accepting, add an epsilon-transition from the new start to the old start, and add epsilon-transitions from each old final state back to the old start; the resulting NFA accepts L*.

Each construction preserves regularity, so all listed languages are accepted by some finite state machine.

Construct an NFA for the reversed language by reversing every transition of an automaton for the original language and swapping start and final states (or using a new start with epsilon-transitions to the old final states); the resulting NFA accepts the reversed strings.

Yes — the complement (with respect to {0,1}*) of a regular language is regular. Take a complete DFA for the language (add a dead state if necessary), then swap accepting and non-accepting states; this DFA recognizes the complement.

Yes — the Kleene closure of a regular language is regular. From an NFA for the language, add a new start state that is accepting and add epsilon-transitions from the new start to the old start and from each old final state back to the old start; the resulting NFA accepts L*.

title: Consider the languages and Which one of the following represents
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Consider the languages L1 = Φ and L2 = {a}. Which one of the following represents L1L2 ∪ L1* ?
solution:
Concept

Three operations on languages govern this problem. (1) Concatenation: for languages X and Y, XY = { xy : x ∈ X, y ∈ Y }; if either factor is the empty set, no pair (x, y) exists, so X·∅ = ∅·Y = ∅. (2) Kleene star: X* = X0 ∪ X1 ∪ X2 ∪ … , and X0 = {ε} by definition (the empty concatenation), so {ε} is ALWAYS a member of any starred language — even ∅* = {ε}. (3) Union just collects the members of both sides.

Application

  1. Evaluate the concatenation L1L2 = Φ·{a}. Since L1 = Φ has no strings, there is no pair to concatenate, so Φ·{a} = Φ.

  2. Evaluate the star L1* = Φ*. The 0-length concatenation contributes ε, so Φ* = {ε}, regardless of Φ being empty.

  3. Take the union: L1L2 ∪ L1* = Φ ∪ {ε} = {ε}.

Cross-check

The expression contains the symbol a only inside L2, which is wiped out the moment it is concatenated with the empty language; nothing else can introduce a, so the result cannot contain any string with a. The star term can only contribute ε. Hence the final language is exactly {ε} — a single-element set containing the empty string, not the empty set and not {ε, a}.

optionFeedback.html: This set consists of a single string — the zero-length string ε — so its cardinality is 1. In language algebra {ε} is the identity element for concatenation: {ε}·Y = Y for every language Y.
This set consists of no strings at all, not even the zero-length string ε, so its cardinality is 0. In language algebra Φ is the annihilator for concatenation: Φ·Y = Φ for every language Y.
This set consists of all strings formed from zero or more copies of a — ε, a, aa, aaa, and so on — so its cardinality is infinite. In language algebra a* is the star of the one-symbol language {a}.

This set consists of two strings — the zero-length string ε and the one-symbol string a — so its cardinality is 2. In language algebra {ε, a} is the union {a}0 ∪ {a}1, the first two power terms of {a}.

title: Consider the following two languages: \(L_1=\{0^i1^j \mid ged (i,j)=1 is
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Consider the following two languages: L_1 = {0^i1^j | gcd(i,j) = 1}. L_2 is any subset of 0^*. Which of the following is correct?

options.html: L_1 is regular and L_2^* is not regular
L_1 is not regular and L_2^* is regular

solution:
CONCEPT

The Myhill–Nerode theorem says that a language is regular exactly when it has finitely many equivalence classes under indistinguishability by suffixes. An infinite family of prefixes separated by suitable suffixes therefore proves non-regularity.

For a unary language, concatenation adds string lengths. Thus the length set of a Kleene star is an additive submonoid of the non-negative integers; every such submonoid is finitely generated, and every nonzero one is eventually periodic. An eventually periodic unary length set is regular.

APPLICATION: THE GCD LANGUAGE

  1. Take the infinite family of prefixes 0^p, one for each prime p.

  2. For distinct primes p and q, append the common suffix 1^q. Then gcd(p,q)=1, so 0^p1^q belongs to L_1, whereas gcd(q,q)=q≠1, so 0^q1^q does not.

  3. The suffix 1^q distinguishes 0^p from 0^q. Infinitely many prime-indexed prefixes are therefore pairwise distinguishable, so L_1 is not regular.

APPLICATION: THE UNARY STAR

  1. Let S={k:0^k∈L_2}. The strings in L_2^* have exactly the lengths in the additive submonoid M=⟨S⟩.

  2. If S is empty or contains no positive length, then M={0} and L_2^*={ε}, which is regular.

  3. Otherwise, M is a nonzero submonoid of the non-negative integers. It has a finite generating set; if d is the gcd of its positive generators, all sufficiently large multiples of d lie in M and no nonmultiple does. Hence membership is eventually periodic with period d.

  4. A DFA handles the finite initial segment explicitly and then tracks the input length modulo d. Therefore L_2^* is regular for every subset L_2 of 0^*.

CROSS-CHECK

  • For p=2 and q=5, the suffix 1^5 gives gcd values 1 and 5 for the prefixes 0^2 and 0^5, demonstrating the distinguishing-suffix mechanism.

  • For L_2={0^6,0^10}, the reachable positive lengths include 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, 20, 22, …; 14 is absent, but every even length from 16 onward is reachable, giving eventual period 2.

  • For L_2={ε}, the star is still {ε}, confirming the zero-length branch.

RESULT

Thus L_1 is not regular and L_2^* is regular, so the saved pair is the correct one.

optionFeedback.html: The common-suffix trace for this pair uses primes 2 and 3: 1^3 gives gcd values 1 and 3 after the prefixes 0^2 and 0^3. The unary-length trace with generators 6 and 10 contains the consecutive even lengths 16, 18, 20, 22, and continues in that residue pattern.

The common-suffix trace for this pair uses primes 3 and 5: 1^5 gives gcd values 1 and 5 after the prefixes 0^3 and 0^5. The unary-length trace with generators 4 and 6 contains every even length from 4 onward.

The common-suffix trace for this pair uses primes 5 and 7: 1^7 gives gcd values 1 and 7 after the prefixes 0^5 and 0^7. The unary-length trace with generators 3 and 5 contains every integer from 8 onward.

The common-suffix trace for this pair uses primes 7 and 11: 1^11 gives gcd values 1 and 11 after the prefixes 0^7 and 0^11. The unary-length trace with generators 8 and 12 contains every multiple of 4 from 8 onward.

text:

Using the pumping lemma, it can be shown that:
solution:
Answer: L1 and L2 are not regular; L3 and L4 are regular.

  • L1 is not regular. Let the pumping length be p and consider s = (ab)^{p+1} a^{p}, which belongs to L1 because the number of (ab) pairs is p+1 and the trailing a-count is p (so p+1 > p). Any decomposition s = xyz with |xy| ≤ p places xy inside the initial (ab)^{...} block (it does not reach the trailing a^{p}). Pumping down (i = 0) removes part of that initial block and yields a string whose initial prefix contains at most p complete "ab" pairs while the trailing a-count remains p, so the condition n > k fails. Thus the pumped string is not in L1, contradicting regularity.

  • L2 is not regular. Let the pumping length be p and take s = a^{p+1} b^{p}, which is in L2 since p+1 ≠ p. Any decomposition with |xy| ≤ p forces y to consist only of a's. Pumping down (i = 0) removes at least one a and can produce a^{p} b^{p}, which has equal numbers of a's and b's and hence is not in L2. This contradicts the pumping lemma for regular languages, so L2 is not regular.

  • L3 is regular. The language restricts the parameter n to a fixed finite range (n ≤ a fixed constant). For each allowed n the set of strings with that n is a regular pattern (a fixed prefix (ab)^{...} followed by a^{k} with k ≥ 1). Since there are only finitely many allowed n values, L3 is a finite union of regular languages and therefore regular.

  • L4 is regular. The condition n ≤ a fixed constant makes L4 a finite language (only finitely many possible values of n), and every finite language is regular.

title: Given grammar XY aA ayb Myhill-Nerode equivalence classes will be:
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Given a grammar
S → XY
X → aA | a
Y → ayb | b
Myhill-Nerode equivalence classes will be:
solution:
Answer: 5 Myhill–Nerode equivalence classes.

Interpretation and language:

Assume the intended productions are X → aX | a (so X generates a+ ) and Y → ayb | b. Then the language generated by S = XY is

L = { a^n b | n ≥ 1 } ∪ { a^m y b | m ≥ 2 }.

Key idea: compute distinct right quotients (residuals) to get Myhill–Nerode classes.

  • Dead residual (no completions): prefixes that already contain a b, or contain a y that cannot be the required y (for example y with fewer than two preceding a's). Right quotient = ∅.

  • Initial residual (no a seen yet): right quotient = a+ b ∪ a^{≥2} y b (this is the full language).

  • Residual after exactly one a: some completions lead to a^+ b forms but not to yb immediately. This residual differs from the 'two-or-more a's' residual because the suffix 'yb' distinguishes them (yb can complete after two-or-more a's but not after exactly one a).

  • Residual after two or more a's (and no y or b yet): right quotient includes both a* b completions and yb completions. This is different from the exactly-one-a residual because it admits the suffix 'yb'.

  • Residual after seeing y that follows two-or-more a's: only b can complete (right quotient = {b}). This is distinct because the suffix 'b' accepts here but a suffix like 'yb' does not apply in the same way to other residuals.

Because these five right quotients are pairwise distinguishable (give distinguishing suffixes such as 'yb' or 'b' or use the empty suffix for the dead residual), the minimal DFA has five states and there are five Myhill–Nerode equivalence classes.

Therefore the correct count is 5.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The language (assuming the intended productions are X → aX | a and Y → ayb | b) is regular and yields five distinct Myhill–Nerode equivalence classes, not four. See the solution for the five different right quotients (dead, zero a's, exactly one a, two-or-more a's, and after y with two-or-more a's).

Incorrect. Three equivalence classes is too few. Distinct situations (no a's yet, exactly one a, at least two a's, a following y after enough a's, and the dead residual) produce five distinguishable right quotients. See the detailed solution.

Correct. There are five Myhill–Nerode equivalence classes. Intuitively: (1) a dead class for prefixes that can never be completed to a string in the language, (2) the initial class (no a yet), (3) after exactly one a, (4) after two or more a's, and (5) after two-or-more a's followed by y (only b can complete). These five right quotients are pairwise distinguishable.

Incorrect. Zero equivalence classes is not possible; even the empty language has one equivalence class (the empty residual). In this grammar the language is nonempty and in fact regular with five distinct equivalence classes. See the full solution for details.

text: Let w be a string defined on the alphabet {0, 1} then which of the following language is regular ?

options.html: L = {wwᴿ | wᴿ is the reverse of w}
L = {w | w has equal number of 0's and 1's}
L = {w | w has even number of 0's and even number of 1's}

solution: The correct answer is Option C. A language is regular if it can be recognized by a finite automaton (DFA). For the set of strings with an even number of 0s and an even number of 1s, we can construct a DFA with four states representing the parity combinations: (even 0s, even 1s), (odd 0s, even 1s), (even 0s, odd 1s), and (odd 0s, odd 1s). The start state is the accepting state for (even, even), and transitions flip the parity bits based on input symbols. Since a finite number of states suffices, this language is regular.\nIn contrast, Option A requires matching the first half of a string with its reverse, which demands unbounded memory to store 'w' for comparison. Option B requires tracking the exact count difference between 0s and 1s, which also exceeds finite memory capabilities. Option D similarly requires counting to ensure the number of 0s strictly exceeds 1s, a task impossible for finite automata. Thus, only Option C represents a regular language.

optionFeedback.html: L = {wwR} (Even Palindromes): To recognize this language, an automaton needs to remember the entire first half of the string (w) in order to match it in reverse order with the second half (wR). Because w can be infinitely long, a DFA would need infinite states. This is a deterministic context-free language (DCFL).

L = {w | w has equal number of 0's and 1's}: A finite automaton cannot count arbitrarily high. To ensure the number of 0's equals the number of 1's, it would have to keep track of the net difference between the two counts. Since the string can have an arbitrarily large number of 0's before a 1 appears, this requires infinite memory.

A language is regular if it can be recognized by a Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA), which has a finite amount of memory.

To track whether a string has an even number of 0's and 1's, we only need to remember the parity (even or odd) of the counts, not the actual counts themselves. Since there are only four possible states of parity, we can easily build a DFA with 4 states:

  1. Even 0's, Even 1's (Start & Accept State)

  2. Even 0's, Odd 1's

  3. Odd 0's, Even 1's

  4. Odd 0's, Odd 1's

Because it requires finite memory, it is a regular language.

title: What is the pumping lemma used for
subject: Theory of Computation
text: What is the pumping lemma used for ?
solution: The pumping lemma is a fundamental tool in formal language theory used to demonstrate that certain languages cannot be recognized by finite automata. Specifically, it provides a necessary condition for regularity: if a language is regular, then there exists a pumping length such that any string longer than this can be 'pumped' (repeatedly generated) while remaining in the language. To use it, we assume a language is regular and then find a specific string that cannot be pumped according to the lemma's rules, thereby deriving a contradiction. This proves the language is not regular.\nOption A is incorrect because the pumping lemma cannot prove a language IS regular; it only helps disprove regularity. Option C is wrong because generating strings is a function of grammars or automata, not the lemma itself. Option D is incorrect as grammar simplification involves removing useless symbols or productions, unrelated to the pumping lemma's purpose. Therefore, Option B is the correct answer.

optionFeedback.html: The pumping lemma is used to prove that a language is not regular. It cannot be used to prove a language is regular.

title: Which of the following statements is True?
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following statements is True?

options.html: Mealy and Moore machines can never have more than 1 final state. They have exactly 1 final state.
Mealy and Moore machines are possible for non-regular languages.
Mealy and Moore machines can be non-deterministic.
Turing Machine (TM) as a transducer is more powerful than Mealy and Moore machines.

solution:
Correct conclusion: The only true statement is the one that says a Turing machine used as a transducer is more powerful than Mealy and Moore machines.

Why the other statements are false:

  • Statement: "Mealy and Moore machines can never have more than 1 final state. They have exactly 1 final state." — False. Mealy and Moore machines are defined as transducers (output-producing finite-state machines), not as language acceptors, so the concept of a single final state does not generally apply.

  • Statement: "Mealy and Moore machines are possible for non-regular languages." — False. Because they have only finite memory, Mealy and Moore machines cannot recognize non-regular languages or perform unbounded counting; they implement regular (rational) functions.

  • Statement: "Mealy and Moore machines can be non-deterministic." — Not in the standard definition. Standard Mealy and Moore machines are deterministic finite-state transducers. Non-deterministic transducer variants can be defined theoretically, but they are not the usual models for single-valued transductions.

  • Statement: "Turing Machine (TM) as a transducer is more powerful than Mealy and Moore machines." — True. A Turing machine has unbounded memory and can compute transformations and decide languages beyond the capability of finite-state transducers.

Takeaway: Mealy and Moore machines are finite-state transducers with finite memory and deterministic standard definitions; they cannot handle non-regular languages. Turing-machine transducers are strictly more powerful due to unbounded memory.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q89
subject: Theory of Computation
text: On what does the output of a Mealy machine depend?
solution:
Concept: A finite state machine’s output can be defined by one of two classical models. In a Mealy machine, the output is a function of BOTH the current input symbol and the present state — written output = λ(present state, current input) — and is associated with each transition (edge) of the state diagram, not with the state itself.

Application: Applying this definition to the item, the output rule matching a Mealy machine is the one requiring the current input together with the present state — the machine reads the input while occupying a particular state, and that combined pair produces the output for that transition.

Contrast with the other rules offered:

  • Only present state describes a Moore machine’s output rule, output = λ(state) alone, evaluated on states rather than on transitions.

  • Only input would make the output a purely combinational function of the input symbol, with no memory of the machine’s current state.

  • Only clock describes the timing signal that synchronizes when a state transition occurs; it governs WHEN a transition happens, not WHAT combination of values determines the output.

Cross-check: In a Mealy machine’s transition table, each (present state, input) cell lists both the next state and an output value — confirming the output is a joint function of the current input and the present state.

optionFeedback.html: Only present state describes an output function λ(state) that depends solely on which state the machine currently occupies, with no reference to the current input symbol.
Only input describes an output function λ(input) that depends solely on the current input symbol, with no reference to which state the machine currently occupies.
current input + Present state describes an output function λ(state, input) that takes both the current state and the current input symbol as its two arguments.
Only clock describes a dependency on the timing signal that drives synchronous state transitions, rather than on the state or input values used to compute an output.

solution:
Concept

In a Mealy machine, each transition carries an output. In an equivalent Moore machine, each state carries one fixed output.

Therefore, a destination state must be split once for each distinct output on transitions entering that state; outgoing outputs are not the splitting criterion.

Application

  1. For q0, the incoming transitions carry outputs y, m, and m. The distinct set is {m, y}, so q0 produces two Moore states: q0,m and q0,y.

  3. For q2, its incoming transition carries output y. The distinct set is {y}, so q2 produces one Moore state: q2,y.

  4. Adding the required state copies gives 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 Moore states.

The four state-output pairs are (q0,m), (q0,y), (q1,m), and (q2,y). Every transition can be redirected to the copy whose state and emitted output match its Mealy destination/output pair, so no additional copy is needed.

Hence, the equivalent Moore machine has 4 states.

title: Consider the following PDA and select the language accepted by
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Consider the following PDA and select the language accepted by PDA from the options.

options.html: The PDA accepts a language which is CFL but not regular

solution:
Concept: A PDA accepts a string by reaching an ACCEPTING (final) state after consuming the whole input — the stack's leftover contents at that moment do not matter unless the diagram forces acceptance to depend on an empty stack. If the START state is ALSO drawn as an accepting state (a double circle), then every string that can be processed by transitions staying inside that state is accepted automatically, regardless of the stack.

Application: Applying this to the diagram:

  1. State A is both the start state and an accepting state; state B is reached only through the optional move (ε, z0 | z), which fires when the stack top is the base marker z0.

  2. A's self-loops cover both input symbols against every possible stack top: reading a symbol that matches the top pushes another copy of it (onto the base marker or onto a matching a/b), and reading a symbol that mismatches the top pops it — so for both a and b, and for every stack top (z0, a, or b), some self-loop transition applies.

  3. Because a transition exists for every (input, stack-top) combination on A, no string over {a,b} can ever get stuck — every string is fully consumed while the automaton stays inside A, which is already an accepting state.

  4. The extra move to B when the stack has returned to z0 only offers an alternate way to accept the balanced strings that A already accepts on its own — it removes nothing from the language.

Cross-check:

  • Empty string (na(w) = nb(w) = 0): accepted immediately since the start state is itself accepting — this already goes against any description that requires the counts to differ.

  • String aab (na(w)=2, nb(w)=1, unequal): a with top z0 pushes a; a with top a pushes a; b with top a pops — fully consumed while staying inside A, so aab is accepted even though its counts are unequal — this goes against any description that requires the counts to be equal.

  • Since every string over {a,b} is accepted this way, the accepted language is the complete set {a,b}*, i.e. (a+b)* — and a language equal to the full set over its alphabet is trivially regular, not a context-free language that fails to be regular.

Correct: the PDA accepts (a+b)*.

optionFeedback.html: This describes only strings where the counts of a and b are equal. But because the start state of the PDA is itself an accepting state, the PDA does not need to reach an empty stack (equal counts) to accept — e.g. reading a, a, b takes the automaton through push, push, pop while remaining in the same accepting state, so this string is accepted despite unequal counts; a description limited to equal counts is too narrow for what this PDA actually accepts.

This describes only strings where the counts of a and b are unequal. But the start state is itself an accepting state, so the empty string — which has equal (zero) counts — is accepted immediately without reading anything; a description that requires the counts to differ excludes a case like this that the PDA does accept.

The start state is both the initial state and an accepting state, and for every possible symbol on top of the stack (the base marker, or a leftover a or b) there is a valid transition for both a and b — pushing when the input matches the top, popping when it does not. So the automaton can process any sequence of a's and b's entirely within that accepting state, never getting stuck; the separate move to the second accepting state when the stack returns to the base marker only adds an alternate way to accept the balanced strings already covered. Every string over {a,b} is therefore accepted.

The push-on-match, pop-on-mismatch transitions look like the classic construction for the equal-count language, which is context-free but not regular — but that classic construction only accepts via reaching an empty stack. Here the start state is itself accepting, so acceptance is not limited to the empty-stack condition; tracing strings with unequal or zero counts of a and b through the loop transitions never forces a rejection, so the language this particular PDA accepts is not the CFL-but-not-regular language that construction usually produces.

title: Consider the following PDA. In above PDA, is starting state
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the following PDA.

In above PDA, A is starting state and F is final state ,the language generated by above PDA is:
solution:
Concept: To find the language a PDA accepts, trace every path from the start state to an accepting state and express the accepted strings as a pattern built from what gets pushed and later popped. If that pattern can already be produced without the stack ever doing indispensable work, the language is regular — in particular, a language that turns out to equal the entire set of strings over the alphabet is always regular, no matter how the machine that generates it is built.

Application: Trace the given PDA state by state:

  1. At A (the start state), the self-loops on 'a' and 'b' read any number of symbols while the stack top stays Z0 — so an arbitrary prefix x ∈ {a,b}* is consumed before anything else happens.

  2. The ε-move A → B fires the moment the stack top is Z0, which is always true here, so control can pass to B after any prefix x — including the empty prefix.

  3. At B, every self-loop rule — whatever the input symbol and whatever is currently on top (Z0, a, or b) — simply pushes the symbol just read on top of the stack. Reading a substring w while in B therefore leaves w's symbols on the stack, with the last symbol of w on top.

  4. The ε-move B → C is enabled for every possible stack top (a, b, or Z0), so B can be left after any number of pushes — including zero, i.e. w may be the empty string.

  5. At C, each self-loop rule reads one input symbol and pops the stack only when it matches the top symbol ('a' pops 'a'; 'b' pops 'b') — this is designed to check the string read while in C against whatever was pushed at B, symbol by symbol, i.e. against w reversed, wR.

  6. The ε-move C → F fires only once the stack top is back to Z0 — that is, only after every symbol pushed at B has been popped at C — and F accepts.

  7. Putting the three phases together, this machine is designed to accept strings of the shape x·w·wR, for x, w ranging freely over {a,b}* — capturing an arbitrary prefix x followed by a block w immediately mirrored by wR.

Because steps 3–6 can be exercised with w chosen as the empty string, x·ε·εR = x for every x — so every string x ∈ {a,b}* is accepted on its own, with no non-trivial push/pop ever required. Since x itself is completely unrestricted, the accepted language is the full set of strings over {a,b}.

Cross-check: A language equal to every possible string over its alphabet is always regular — a single-state automaton that stays in its (accepting) state on every symbol already recognises it, no stack required. A concrete check confirms it too: the string 'aba' is accepted by taking x = 'aba' and w = ε, using only the A-state loop — no push/pop phase is even needed.

Result: The language accepted by this PDA is L = (a + b)* — every string over {a,b} — which is Regular.

optionFeedback.html: Because the middle push-and-match phase can be exercised with nothing on it (an empty portion), every string over {a,b} has an accepting run — the language is the full set (a+b)*, and any language equal to the whole alphabet is regular by definition.

The opening state's self-loop reads any number of a's or b's before any stack activity begins, so strings of every length reach an accepting computation — a finite language cannot contain strings of unbounded length, so this classification does not hold.

This label treats having a state whose pop rule requires an exact symbol match as sufficient by itself to place the accepted language outside what a finite-state device can recognise. But that inference doesn't hold in general — plenty of machines with an exact-match pop rule built into their design still end up recognising very simple languages; you cannot read off a language's classification from one state's transition style without separately analysing what the complete machine, across all its states and transitions, actually accepts.

This label assumes that because control can leave state B for state C via more than one competing ε-transition, resolving that choice one way rather than another must change which strings get accepted — treating the mere presence of a nondeterministic branch point as proof that determinism would lose information. But a machine having multiple nondeterministic paths on offer doesn't automatically mean the accepted language depends on which path is taken; that has to be verified directly rather than assumed from the diagram's branching alone.

title: Which of the following is False?
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following is False?

options.html: Regular expressions are used for pattern matching.
Lexical analyzers in compilers are implemented by DFA.
FA + finite stack is more powerful than finite automata.
NFA + stack is more powerful than DFA + stack.

solution:
Answer: The false statement is "FA + finite stack is more powerful than finite automata."

  • Regular expressions are used for pattern matching. (True) Regular expressions describe regular languages and are widely used to specify and search for patterns (including tokens in lexical analysis).

  • Lexical analyzers in compilers are implemented by DFA. (True) Regular expressions for tokens are converted to NFAs and then to DFAs; the DFA is used to perform fast, deterministic token recognition.

  • FA + finite stack is more powerful than finite automata. (False) If the stack is bounded (finite number of possible stack contents), the machine still has only finitely many configurations. Therefore a finite stack does not increase computational power and the model remains equivalent to a finite automaton.

  • NFA + stack is more powerful than DFA + stack. (True) An NFA with an unbounded stack corresponds to a nondeterministic pushdown automaton (NPDA) and a DFA with an unbounded stack corresponds to a deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA). Nondeterministic pushdown automata can recognize some context-free languages that deterministic pushdown automata cannot, so the nondeterministic model is strictly more expressive in general.

Conclusion: The statement about a finite stack increasing power is false; all other statements are true.

optionFeedback.html: True — Regular expressions describe regular languages and are commonly used for pattern matching in text processing and for specifying token patterns in lexical analysis.
True — Lexical analyzers are typically implemented as deterministic finite automata generated from regular expressions (possibly after conversion from nondeterministic finite automata).

False — A finite automaton augmented with a stack that is bounded in size (a finite stack) does not increase the machine's computational power. Because the stack can take only finitely many values, the overall machine still has finitely many configurations and is equivalent to a finite automaton.

True — A nondeterministic finite automaton with an unbounded stack corresponds to a nondeterministic pushdown automaton (NPDA), while a deterministic finite automaton with an unbounded stack corresponds to a deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA). NPDA can recognize some context-free languages that DPDA cannot, so the nondeterministic version is more powerful in that sense.
