title: Which of the following languages is ambiguous (MSQ)
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Q. Which of the following languages is ambiguous ?

options.html: L = { am bn cp ∣ m = n or n = p }
L = { am bn cp ∣ m > n and m < n }
L = { am bn cp dq ∣ m = q or n = p}
L = { am bm cn dn ∣ m,n ≥ 0 } ∪ { am bn cn dm ∣ m,n ≥ 0 }.

solution:
Answer:

The ambiguous languages are:

  • L = { a^m b^n c^p | m = n or n = p }

  • L = { a^m b^n c^p d^q | m = q or n = p }

  • L = { a^m b^m c^n d^n | m,n ≥ 0 } ∪ { a^m b^n c^n d^m | m,n ≥ 0 }

Reason:

  1. Each listed language is a union of two context-free languages whose intersection is nonempty and contains strings with equal repeated counts in corresponding positions (for example, a^k b^k c^k or a^k b^k c^k d^k).

  2. Any string in that intersection can be generated by either component of the union, giving two different parse trees. Therefore any context-free grammar for the union will be ambiguous for those strings; these are standard examples of inherently ambiguous context-free languages.

  3. The only non-ambiguous choice among the options is the one with the impossible condition m > n and m < n, which yields the empty language; the empty language does not exhibit ambiguity.

Example to illustrate ambiguity:

  • For L = { a^m b^n c^p | m = n or n = p }, the string a b c (i.e. a^1 b^1 c^1) belongs to both components (1=1 in both equalities) and so has two distinct derivations—one using the m = n rule and one using the n = p rule.

  • Similarly, for the four-symbol languages, the string a b c d (a^1 b^1 c^1 d^1) lies in the intersection and is derivable from either component, producing two parse trees.

Conclusion: The ambiguous languages in the list are the three unions described above; the language with the contradictory condition is empty and not ambiguous.

optionFeedback.html: The language is the union of { a^m b^m c^p : m,p ≥ 0 } and { a^m b^n c^n : m,n ≥ 0 }. Their intersection contains strings of the form a^k b^k c^k (for k ≥ 0). Any context-free grammar that generates the union will give two distinct parse trees for such strings (one coming from each component), so the language is ambiguous (in fact, this is a standard inherently ambiguous example).
The condition m > n and m < n cannot hold simultaneously, so the set is empty. The empty language does not exhibit ambiguity (it contains no strings to parse), so this language is not ambiguous.

This language is the union of { a^m b^n c^p d^m : m,n,p ≥ 0 } and { a^m b^n c^n d^q : m,n,q ≥ 0 } (re-expressed to show components). Their intersection contains strings where m = q and n = p, for example a^k b^k c^k d^k. Such strings can be generated by either component, giving two different parse trees. Hence the language is ambiguous (this is a standard inherently ambiguous construction for four symbols).

This language is the union of { a^m b^m c^n d^n } and { a^m b^n c^n d^m }. The intersection contains strings a^k b^k c^k d^k; such strings have two distinct derivations (one from each half of the union), so the language is ambiguous. This is a standard example of an inherently ambiguous CFL.

text:

options.html: L₁ and L₃ are not CFL but L₂ and L₄ are CFLs

solution: L₁: This language is not context-free. A context-free grammar (CFG) can only keep track of a limited number of "dependencies" between symbols. It can only maintain equality between two counts. L₄: This language is context-free. The number of 'a's is independent of the 'b's and 'c's. The CFG can generate any number of 'a's, and independently generate 'b's and 'c's where the number of 'c's is twice the number of 'b's. title: Which of the following is true?
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following is true?

options.html: L={wzwr | w ∊ {0,1}* and z ∊ {0,1} } is a CFL but not DCFL
L={0w 1x 2y 3z | w=y or x=z & w, x, y ,z >0 } is a CFL but not DCFL
L={axb2xcx | x>0} is CSL but not CFL
L={axbycydx | x, y>0} is CSL but not CFL

solution:
Correct statements (from the given options): The two true descriptions are the ones about the odd-length palindrome language and the a^x b^{2x} c^x language.

  • L = { w z w^r | w ∈ {0,1}*, z ∈ {0,1} } is a context-free language but not a deterministic context-free language.

    Reason (CFL): This is the set of odd-length palindromes over {0,1}; a CFG such as S -> 0S0 | 1S1 | 0 | 1 generates it.

    Reason (not DCFL): A deterministic pushdown automaton cannot in general decide deterministically where to switch from pushing to popping if the single center symbol is not a unique marker; nondeterminism is needed to guess the midpoint.

  • L = { a^x b^{2x} c^x | x > 0 } is not context-free but is context-sensitive.

    Reason: Use a homomorphism argument. Let h be the homomorphism that maps a->a, c->c and a new symbol B->bb. Then h({ a^n B^n c^n }) = { a^n b^{2n} c^n }. The language { a^n B^n c^n } (equivalent to a^n b^n c^n up to renaming) is a standard non-context-free language, so { a^n b^{2n} c^n } is not context-free. It is context-sensitive because a linear-bounded automaton can check the required equalities.

  • The statement about L = { 0^w 1^x 2^y 3^z | w = y or x = z, w,x,y,z > 0 } is ambiguous and needs careful parsing.

    If intended as the union of two languages (either 0-count equals 2-count, or 1-count equals 3-count), each disjunct is CFL and their union is CFL. If the intent was to require simultaneous comparisons of independent counts in non-nested order, that leads to a language requiring more power than a single-stack PDA and may not be context-free. Clarify the intended logical grouping to decide correctly.

  • L = { a^x b^y c^y d^x | x,y > 0 } is context-free (so the claim that it is context-sensitive but not context-free is false).

    Reason: A CFG can generate these strings by nesting the outer a/d matching and generating the inner b/c matching independently, for example S -> a S d | T and T -> b T c | b c.

Final selection: The true option statements are the ones asserting that the odd-length palindrome language is CFL but not DCFL, and that the a^x b^{2x} c^x language is context-sensitive but not context-free.

optionFeedback.html: The language L = { w z w^r | w ∈ {0,1}* and z ∈ {0,1} } is context-free because it is the set of odd-length palindromes over {0,1} (a CFG like S -> 0S0 | 1S1 | 0 | 1 generates it). It is not deterministic context-free because a deterministic pushdown automaton cannot in general decide deterministically where the left half ends and the right half (the reverse) begins when the center symbol z is not uniquely identifiable; a nondeterministic PDA can guess the midpoint and then pop to match the reverse, but a DPDA cannot reliably make that choice for all inputs.

The statement is not correct as written. The language requires comparing counts in non-nested positions (either number of 0s equals number of 2s, or number of 1s equals number of 3s). If the intent were a union of two simple equalities (strings where 0-count equals 2-count OR where 1-count equals 3-count), each individual condition gives a CFL, and the union of CFLs is a CFL. However, if the language is intended to require both equalities or to force simultaneously comparing two independent counts in the non-nested order 0^w 1^x 2^y 3^z, that requires more power than a single-stack PDA and is not context-free. The original problem statement is ambiguous; clarify whether the condition is a union (OR) or a conjunction (AND).

The language L = { a^x b^{2x} c^x | x > 0 } is not context-free but is context-sensitive. A simple way to see it is via a homomorphism trick: let h map a->a, c->c, and map a new symbol B to bb. Then h({ a^n B^n c^n }) = { a^n b^{2n} c^n }. The language { a^n B^n c^n } is equivalent (up to renaming) to { a^n b^n c^n }, which is a standard non-context-free language. Because CFLs are closed under inverse homomorphism, if { a^n b^{2n} c^n } were context-free then its inverse under h would be context-free, which it is not. Hence { a^x b^{2x} c^x } is not CFL; it is context-sensitive (it can be recognized by a linear-bounded automaton).

The language L = { a^x b^y c^y d^x | x,y > 0 } is context-free. A CFG can generate it by nesting the outer a/d pair and the inner b/c pair independently, for example: S -> a S d | T, T -> b T c | b c. This produces strings of the form a^x (b^y c^y) d^x, so the language is CFL. Therefore the claim that it is context-sensitive but not context-free is incorrect.

title: Consider the given languages: {0p1q0r p,q,r {0p1q0r p+q and {0p1q0r1s
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the given languages:

L1: {0p1q0r | p,q,r ≥ 0}

L2: {0p1q0r | p+q = r and p > 0}

L3: {0p1q0r1s | p+r = q+s and p > 0}

Which of the following is/are true about the above languages:

options.html: L1 is regular and L3 is DCFL
L2 is CFL and L3 is CSL
L2 is CFL and L3 is CSL
Complement of L1 is CFL but not regular

solution:
L1: L1 = {0^p 1^q 0^r | p,q,r ≥ 0}. This equals the regular language 0*1*0*, so L1 is regular.

L2: L2 = {0^p 1^q 0^r | p+q = r and p > 0}. L2 is a context-free language. Sketch of a PDA:

  • 1) Read the first block of zeros (require at least one); push one stack symbol for each 0.

  • 2) Read the block of ones; push one stack symbol for each 1.

  • 3) On the final block of zeros pop exactly one stack symbol per 0. If the stack is empty at the end, accept. This enforces r = p+q.

L3: L3 = {0^p 1^q 0^r 1^s | p+r = q+s and p > 0}. L3 is context-sensitive but not context-free.

  • Why L3 is context-sensitive: a linear-bounded automaton (LBA) can verify p+r = q+s using only linear workspace. For example, repeatedly find an unmarked 0 in the first or third block and an unmarked 1 in the second or fourth block and mark them both; when no unmarked symbols remain, accept iff both sides are exhausted. This marking/cancellation uses only the input tape (bounded workspace), so L3 is CSL.

  • Why L3 is not context-free (sketch): L3 contains the subset {0^n 1^n 0^n 1^n | n > 0}, which requires enforcing two separate equalities across distant blocks; such languages are known not to be context-free by standard pumping/closure arguments. Therefore L3 is not CFL.

Conclusion: The correct classification is that L1 is regular, L2 is context-free, and L3 is context-sensitive (not context-free). Therefore the statements that assert L2 is CFL and L3 is CSL are correct; the other statements are incorrect.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The first part is right: L1 = {0^p 1^q 0^r | p,q,r ≥ 0} = 0*1*0*, so L1 is regular. The second claim is wrong: L3 is not a deterministic context-free language. L3 requires comparing sums across separated blocks (p + r versus q + s), which goes beyond deterministic CFL power; L3 is context-sensitive rather than a DCFL.

Correct. L2 = {0^p 1^q 0^r | p+q = r and p > 0} is context-free: a pushdown automaton can (1) read and push one stack symbol for each 0 in the first block (requiring at least one), (2) push one symbol for each 1 in the second block, and then (3) on the final block of zeros pop one stack symbol per 0; acceptance occurs when the stack is empty. L3 = {0^p 1^q 0^r 1^s | p+r = q+s and p>0} is context-sensitive: a linear-bounded automaton can repeatedly match and cross off one 0 from the first or third block with one 1 from the second or fourth block until no symbols remain, verifying p+r = q+s. This requires only linear workspace, so L3 is CSL (and not CFL).

Correct (same as previous): L2 is context-free using a PDA that pushes for each 0 in the first block and for each 1 in the second block, then pops one symbol per 0 in the final block to ensure r = p+q (and p>0 ensures the first block is nonempty). L3 is context-sensitive: an LBA can verify p+r = q+s by repeatedly marking off matching 0/1 pairs across the blocks, so L3 is CSL (not CFL).

Incorrect. The complement of L1 is regular. Since L1 is regular (0*1*0*), regular languages are closed under complement, so the complement is also regular (and therefore also a CFL). The claim that the complement is CFL but not regular is false.

(P) (L = {w∈{0,1}* | w is a binary number divisible by 3})

(1) Context-Free, but not Regular

(Q) (L = {wwR | w∈{a,b}*})

(2) Recursive, but not Context-Free

(R) (L = {w | w is a C program that halts on every input})

(3) Regular

(S) (L = {an bm ck | n=m or m=k})

(4) Not Recursively Enumerable
solution:
Concept: Formal languages form a strict containment hierarchy — Regular ⊂ Context-Free ⊂ Recursive ⊂ Recursively Enumerable. A language is Regular exactly when a finite-state machine with fixed, finite memory accepts it (or the pumping lemma disproves it). It is Context-Free when a pushdown automaton — finite control plus one unbounded stack — accepts it, or when it is assembled from known context-free languages via closure properties such as union. A language fails to be Recursive when no algorithm decides membership — undecidability, shown via Rice's theorem or a reduction from the Halting Problem. Some undecidable languages remain Recursively Enumerable (semi-decidable); others fail to be RE at all, when even semi-deciding membership would require checking infinitely many sub-instances that no single procedure can certify — placing them above RE/co-RE in the arithmetic hierarchy.

Application:

  • (P) L = {w ∈ {0,1}* | w is a binary number divisible by 3}: tracking the remainder mod 3 while reading bits left to right needs only 3 states (remainder 0, 1, 2), with every incoming bit causing one deterministic transition — exactly a DFA (taking the empty string as the encoding of 0, which is divisible by 3, so the start/remainder-0 state is consistently accepting). So P is Regular.

  • (Q) L = {wwR | w ∈ {a,b}*}: this is the set of even-length strings whose second half exactly mirrors the first. A pushdown automaton pushes the first half onto its stack, guesses the midpoint, then pops while matching the second half; no fixed number of states can bound how long that first half is, so no DFA can accept it. Hence Q is Context-Free but not Regular.

  • (R) L = {w | w encodes a program that halts on every possible input} (the totality problem): by Rice's theorem, since 'halts on every input' is a nontrivial semantic property of the program's behaviour, TOTAL is undecidable. Beyond undecidability, TOTAL is also known to sit strictly above both RE and co-RE in the arithmetic hierarchy (it is Π2-complete) — verifying it would require confirming termination on every one of infinitely many inputs, which no single semi-decision procedure can certify either way. So R is Not Recursively Enumerable.

  • (S) L = {an bm ck | n=m or m=k}: this is exactly the union of {an bn ck} and {an bm cm}. Each piece is Context-Free (a single stack matches one adjacent pair of exponents while the third symbol's count runs free), and the class of Context-Free languages is closed under union, so S is Context-Free. To see S is not Regular, intersect it with the regular language a+b+ (one-or-more a's then one-or-more b's, no c's): inside S this forces n=m (since k=0 rules out the m=k branch once m≥1), giving exactly {an bn | n≥1} — the textbook non-regular language. Since regular languages are closed under intersection with another regular language, S itself cannot be Regular (else this intersection would be Regular too).

Cross-check: the 3-state DFA for P correctly rejects 5 (1012, remainder 2) and accepts 6 (1102, remainder 0), confirming the construction. For Q, take w = apb, so s = wwR = apbb ap (an even-length member of L for any pumping length p). Pumping lemma: any split with |xy|≤p and |y|≥1 has y consisting only of leading a's; pumping down shrinks the FIRST a-block but leaves the second a-block at length p, breaking the equal-block symmetry wwR requires — so the pumped string leaves L, confirming Q cannot be Regular, while the push-then-pop PDA independently confirms it is accepted. For R, Rice's theorem already gives undecidability; separately, TOTAL is the standard example used to show a language can be undecidable yet still fail to be RE or co-RE (it is Π2-complete in the arithmetic hierarchy) — confirming the classification is specifically 'Not Recursively Enumerable', not simply 'undecidable'. For S, intersecting with the regular language a+b+ isolates {an bn} (fails the pumping lemma for regularity, a standard fact); since intersection with a regular set preserves regularity, S cannot itself be Regular, while the same substitution keeps it inside the {n=m} disjunct (a CFL), so both boundary checks agree with the classification above.

Result: Matching each entry to its class: P → Regular, Q → Context-Free (not Regular), R → Not Recursively Enumerable, S → Context-Free (not Regular). This is the pairing P-3, Q-1, R-4, S-1.

Together these give P-3, Q-1, R-4, S-1.

This pairing overshoots on P: divisibility by 3 needs only three DFA states (tracking the remainder), so no stack is required — it does not need Context-Free power. It also undershoots on Q: a stack that pushes the first half and pops while matching the reversed second half already accepts wwR, so it does not need more than pushdown power. And it undershoots on S: intersecting S with the regular language a+b+ (one-or-more a's then one-or-more b's, no c's) forces n=m, giving exactly {an bn | n≥1} inside it; since intersecting a Regular language with another Regular language must itself stay Regular, and {an bn} fails the pumping lemma, S cannot collapse to a finite-state (Regular) language.

It also understates R: whether a program halts on every input is a property no algorithm can even semi-decide; Rice's theorem makes it undecidable, and it sits above both RE and co-RE, well beyond the pushdown-recognizable level. And it overshoots on S: S is the union of an bn ck and an bm cm, each matched with a single stack, and unions of Context-Free languages stay Context-Free, so nothing here needs going beyond that class.

This pairing overshoots specifically on its S mapping: S is built as the union of an bn ck and an bm cm, and each piece needs only one stack to match one pair of exponents while the third symbol's count runs free. title: Identify the language which is DCFL:
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Identify the language L which is DCFL:
solution:
Answer: All four languages I, II, III and IV are deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs).

  • I. L = {0^m 1^n 2^k 3^l | m = n or k = l}: A deterministic PDA can handle this because the input is split into fixed symbol blocks and the two equality checks concern disjoint symbol pairs (0/1 and 2/3). Implement the PDA so that the stack region used during the 0/1 phase is separated from the region used during the 2/3 phase (use a special separator symbol on the stack when switching phases). The PDA pushes one symbol per 0 and pops for each 1; it also uses a distinct symbol set for the 2/3 comparison. At the end the PDA accepts if either the 0/1 region indicates equality or the 2/3 region indicates equality. Because the symbol blocks and stack regions are managed deterministically, this is a DCFL.

  • II. L = {0^m 1^n 2^k 3^l | n = k and m = l} = {0^m 1^n 2^n 3^m}: Construct a deterministic PDA that, while reading the 0s, pushes a symbol A for each 0; while reading the 1s it pushes a different symbol B for each 1. In the 2-block the PDA pops one B for each 2; in the 3-block it pops one A for each 3. The order of pushes and pops (first all B pops, then A pops) matches the input order, so all operations are deterministic. The PDA accepts iff the stack is empty at the end.

  • III. L = {a^n b^n c^{2n} | n ≥ 1}: A deterministic PDA can implement this by turning each matched a–b pair into two c-tokens on the stack. Concretely, push X for each a. For each b, pop one X and push two C markers. Then for each c pop a single C marker. After processing all c's the stack should be empty. All actions are driven by the current input symbol and top-of-stack and so are deterministic.

  • IV. L = {a^n b^m | 2n ≤ m ≤ 3n}: Use a deterministic stack layout that associates, for each a, a small block of stack symbols (for example push a separator S and three Xs: SXXX). While reading b’s the PDA pops one X per b; trying to pop beyond the available Xs causes rejection (ensures m ≤ 3n). At the end use the S separators to deterministically check that the number of leftover Xs does not exceed the number of S blocks (this enforces m ≥ 2n equivalently). Because blocks and separators are processed in a fixed left-to-right order, the PDA can perform these checks deterministically.

Summary: each language admits a deterministic PDA construction (push and pop patterns are tied to fixed input blocks and use distinct stack symbols or separators), so all four are DCFLs.

Each of I–IV can be recognized by a deterministic pushdown automaton because the required comparisons occur in fixed blocks of the input and can be implemented deterministically using stack symbols and separators.

Incorrect. The choice "III, IV only" is incomplete: languages I and II are also deterministic context-free. In particular, I and II admit straightforward deterministic PDA constructions (I uses separate stack regions for the 0/1 and 2/3 comparisons; II pushes one symbol per 0 and another per 1 and pops them in the 2 and 3 blocks respectively).

Incorrect. The choice "I, III, IV only" misses language II, which is also a DCFL. Language II (strings of the form 0^m1^n2^n3^m) can be recognized deterministically by pushing one symbol per 0, pushing a different symbol per 1, popping the second symbol for each 2, and finally popping the first symbol for each 3 — all done in a single left-to-right deterministic pass.

Correct. The choice "All are DCFL" is right. Each language I–IV can be recognized by a deterministic pushdown automaton because the equalities/inequalities involve counts in fixed, separate blocks and can be implemented deterministically with appropriate stack symbols and separators. title: Find the non-context free language among the following.
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Find the non-context free language among the following.
solution:
To determine which language is not context-free, we analyze each option based on the properties of context-free languages (CFLs). CFLs can be recognized by pushdown automata (PDAs), which use a stack to handle nested or matching structures.

Option A: L = {ωωR ∣ ω ∈ {0,1}∗}

This language consists of palindromes over {0,1}. A PDA can recognize palindromes by pushing symbols onto the stack until the middle, then popping and matching with the reverse. This is a classic context-free language.

Option B: L = {p^n q^n ∣ n ≥ 0}

This language requires matching equal numbers of p and q symbols. A PDA can push a symbol for each p and pop for each q. This is a standard context-free language.

Option C: L = {ωω ∣ ω ∈ {0,1}∗}

This language consists of strings formed by repeating a string twice. A PDA cannot compare the first half with the second half because it cannot store the entire first half in the stack and then compare it with the second half. This language is not context-free.

Option D: L = {p^n q^m r^m s^n ∣ n,m ≥ 0}

This language has two independent matching pairs: p and s must have the same count, and q and r must have the same count. A PDA can use the stack to count p's and then match with s's, and similarly for q and r. This is context-free.

Option E: Question not attempted

This is not a valid language definition and does not represent a formal language. It is not considered in the analysis.

Therefore, the only language that is not context-free is Option C.

यह भाषा {0,1} पर पलिंड्रोमों से बनी है। एक PDA पलिंड्रोम को पहचान सकता है जब तक कि वह स्टैक में पहले आधे भाग के प्रत्येक प्रतीक को डालता है और फिर दूसरे आधे भाग के प्रत्येक प्रतीक के साथ मिलाता है। यह एक मानक संदर्भ-मुक्त भाषा है।

विकल्प B: L = {p^n q^n ∣ n ≥ 0}

इस भाषा में p और q की संख्या बराबर होनी चाहिए। एक PDA प्रत्येक p के लिए एक प्रतीक डाल सकता है और प्रत्येक q के लिए एक प्रतीक निकाल सकता है। यह एक मानक संदर्भ-मुक्त भाषा है।

विकल्प C: L = {ωω ∣ ω ∈ {0,1}∗}

यह भाषा एक शब्द को दो बार दोहराने से बनी है। एक PDA पहले आधे भाग को दूसरे आधे भाग के साथ तुलना नहीं कर सकता क्योंकि यह पूरे पहले आधे भाग को स्टैक में स्टोर नहीं कर सकता और फिर दूसरे आधे भाग के साथ तुलना कर सकता है। यह भाषा संदर्भ-मुक्त नहीं है।

विकल्प D: L = {p^n q^m r^m s^n ∣ n,m ≥ 0}

इस भाषा में दो स्वतंत्र मैचिंग जोड़े हैं: p और s की संख्या बराबर होनी चाहिए, और q और r की संख्या बराबर होनी चाहिए। एक PDA स्टैक का उपयोग कर सकता है p की संख्या गिनने और फिर s के साथ मिलान करने के लिए, और इसी तरह q और r के लिए। यह संदर्भ-मुक्त है।

यह एक वैध भाषा परिभाषा नहीं है और इसे विश्लेषण में नहीं लिया जाता है।

title: Consider CFG with no ϵ-productions. Let be the maximum number
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Q. Consider a CFG G with no ϵ-productions. Let k be the maximum number of symbols on the right-hand side of any production in G, ∣P∣ be the number of productions, and ∣T∣ be the number of terminals. Let G′ be the equivalent grammar in Chomsky Normal Form (CNF).

  1. If G has no null productions, then the maximum number of productions in the CNF equivalent of G is (k−1)∣P∣+∣T∣.

  2. The maximum height of the parse tree of any string generated by G′ is at most 2k−1, where k is the maximum number of symbols on the RHS of G.

Choose the correct option: (MCQ)
solution:
Answer: Both statements are False.

Statement 1 — "Maximum number of productions in CNF = (k−1)|P| + |T|":

False. Reason:

  • CNF conversion replaces each RHS of length r by r−1 binary productions, so summing (r−1) over productions gives at most (k−1)|P| for those binary rules. But this accounting omits effects of other steps.

  • Introducing variables to replace terminals contributes at most |T| new terminal rules, but those new variables also appear in binary rules, which the simple formula does not fully count.

  • Crucially, elimination of unit productions can cause long RHS productions to be copied to many nonterminals. Example: if A1 → A2 → ... → An and An → X1 X2 ... Xk, then removing unit productions will add the long RHS to A1, A2, ..., increasing the total number of productions well beyond (k−1)|P| + |T|.

  • Therefore the stated formula is not a guaranteed maximum; it can underestimate the total after full CNF conversion.

Statement 2 — "The maximum height of the parse tree of any string generated by G′ is at most 2k−1, where k is the maximum number of symbols on the RHS of G":

False. Reason:

  • The bound 2k−1 correctly describes the height contributed when a single long RHS of length k is rewritten as a binary tree during CNF conversion (the binary decomposition of that one production).

  • However, whole derivations may apply such productions repeatedly and can nest many such decompositions. For grammars that allow repeated nesting (for example a nonterminal that expands into k nonterminals that again each expand similarly), the parse-tree height grows with the number of nesting steps and can be arbitrarily large.

  • A simple counterexample: a grammar with a recursive production like S → S S (a case with k = 2) yields parse trees whose height increases with the number of derivation steps; there is no absolute bound 2k−1 on the height of all generated strings.

  • Thus 2k−1 is only the size of the local expansion for one production, not a global upper bound for all parse trees of G′.

Summary: Both statements are false. Statement 1 underestimates possible growth caused by unit-production elimination and other CNF steps; Statement 2 confuses the local expansion of one production with the global height of arbitrary derivations.

text: A CFG(Context Free Grammar) is said to be in Chomsky Normal Form (CNF), if all the productions are of the form A -> BC or A -> a. Let G be a CFG in CNF. To derive a string of terminals of length x, the number of products to be used is , ISRO 2018
solution: In Chomsky Normal Form (CNF), every production rule is either A -> BC or A -> a. To derive a string of length x, we need exactly x terminal productions (A -> a). Additionally, to combine these x terminals into a single start symbol using binary rules (A -> BC), we need x - 1 binary productions. Thus, the total number of productions used is x + (x - 1) = 2x - 1.

title: The grammar aSb aS generates the language
subject: Theory of Computation
text: The grammar S → aSb | aS | € generates the language
solution:
Answer: {a^m b^n | m ≥ n, m,n ≥ 0}

  • S → ε yields the empty string (m = 0, n = 0).

  • S → aS adds one 'a' (increases m by 1) without adding any 'b'.

  • S → aSb adds one 'a' and one 'b' (increases both m and n by 1).

  • Because b's are only produced together with matching a's and aS can add extra a's, the number of a's is always at least the number of b's, and all a's occur before all b's. Hence all generated strings are of the form a^m b^n with m ≥ n.

  • Examples: ε, a, ab, aa, aab, aabb, aaa, aabbb is not generated because it has more b's than a's.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The grammar generates all strings of the form a^m b^n with m ≥ n (m,n ≥ 0). S → ε gives the empty string; S → aS adds an extra a (increasing m); S → aSb adds one a and one b (increasing both m and n). Therefore there can never be more b's than a's, and all a's appear before all b's.

Incorrect. The grammar cannot produce more b's than a's. The only rule that produces b's is aSb, which always pairs each produced b with a corresponding a to its left, so the number of b's cannot exceed the number of a's.

Incorrect. While the rule aSb can produce equal numbers of a's and b's, the rule aS allows extra a's to be added without producing b's. Thus the grammar permits more a's than b's, so equality of counts is not required.

title: Consider the statements below: Matching of parenthesis. Syntax of nested
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the statements below:
S1: Matching of parenthesis.
S2: Syntax of nested if-else.
S3: Matching of Lvalue and Rvalue S1, S2 and S3 are features.
Which of the above features cannot be performed by a Context free grammar?
solution:
Answer: Only S3 (Matching of Lvalue and Rvalue) cannot be performed by a Context-Free Grammar.

  • S1 — Matching of parentheses: This is a classic context-free construct (balanced parentheses). A CFG can generate balanced pairs using recursion, and a pushdown automaton can recognize it.

  • S2 — Syntax of nested if-else: The nested-if syntax is describable by a CFG. Although grammars for if-else can be ambiguous (the dangling-else problem), the ambiguity is resolved by grammar rewriting or parser disambiguation; the construct itself remains context-free.

  • S3 — Matching of Lvalue and Rvalue (type checking): This requires context-sensitive information such as declared types, scope, and symbol-table lookups. A CFG cannot enforce that an assigned expression has a compatible type with the variable being assigned.

Example: parsing will accept statements like char x; x = 10; syntactically, but detecting that assigning an integer literal to a char (or incompatible types generally) is a semantic/type error requires semantic analysis or syntax-directed translation (SDT), not a CFG.

Conclusion: Use a context-free grammar for describing and parsing S1 and S2 (syntax). Use semantic analysis/SDT (context-sensitive checks) to perform S3 (type and Lvalue/Rvalue matching).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Matching of parentheses (S1) and the syntax of nested if-else (S2) are context-free constructs that a context-free grammar can describe (for example, balanced parentheses can be generated by a recursive rule). The matching of Lvalue and Rvalue types (S3) requires context-sensitive information (type information and symbol-table checks) and must be handled by semantic analysis or syntax-directed translation.

Correct. Type matching between Lvalue and Rvalue (S3) is a semantic, context-sensitive check that a context-free grammar cannot enforce. Matching parentheses (S1) and nested if-else syntax (S2) can be described by CFGs; type checks are performed later during semantic analysis or using syntax-directed translation.

Incorrect. While type matching between Lvalue and Rvalue (S3) cannot be enforced by a CFG, the syntax of nested if-else (S2) can be handled by a context-free grammar. Therefore, saying both S2 and S3 cannot be performed by a CFG is wrong—only the type-matching feature (S3) requires semantic/context-sensitive checks.

Incorrect. The syntax of nested if-else (S2) can be expressed by a context-free grammar (ambiguity like the dangling-else can be resolved by grammar rewriting or parser rules). The feature that cannot be enforced by a CFG is matching Lvalue and Rvalue types (S3), which requires semantic checks and a symbol table.

title: Consider the following CFG, S→aA∣bSS∣SS A→aAb∣bAa∣AA∣ϵ The language generated by
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the following CFG, G:

S→aA∣bSS∣SS

A→aAb∣bAa∣AA∣ϵ

The language generated by G is:

options.html: Set of all strings with at least one 'a'
Set of all strings with at least two 'a's
Set of all strings with at least one more 'a' than the number of 'b's

solution:
Grammar:

S → aA | bSS | SS

A → aAb | bAa | AA | ε

Key observation: the nonterminal A generates exactly the strings with an equal number of 'a's and 'b's.

  • Reason for A: ε has equal numbers (zero). The productions aAb and bAa add one 'a' and one 'b' in opposite ends, preserving equality. Concatenation AA also preserves equality, so every string generated by A has #a = #b.

  • Define f(w) = number of 'a's minus number of 'b's. For any string from A, f = 0.

  • S → aA gives strings with f = 1 (one extra 'a' plus a string from A with f = 0).

  • If two strings have f-values x and y from S, then SS yields a string with f = x + y, and bSS yields f = -1 + x + y. Since the base value 1 is achievable, closure under these productions yields all positive integers for f.

  • In particular, f can never be 0 or negative for strings from S, and f = 1 is the minimum possible value, so every S-derived string satisfies f ≥ 1.

Conclusion: The language generated by the grammar is exactly the set of strings where the number of 'a's exceeds the number of 'b's by at least one (i.e., #a(w) = #b(w) + k for some integer k ≥ 1).

Example counterexamples: the single-letter string "a" is in the language (S → aA, A → ε), so any description that requires at least two 'a's is too restrictive. A string like "bbabb" has one 'a' but more 'b's and cannot be produced by the grammar, so descriptions that allow such strings are too permissive.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. This description is too weak: it permits strings that have at least one 'a' but still have more 'b's than 'a's. For example, the string "bbabb" contains one 'a' and more 'b's, but such strings cannot be derived from the grammar because every string derived from the start symbol has strictly more 'a's than 'b's.
Incorrect. The grammar can generate the single-letter string "a" (S → aA, A → ε), which has only one 'a'. Therefore the set requiring at least two 'a's is too restrictive.

Correct. Brief explanation: the nonterminal A generates exactly those strings with an equal number of 'a's and 'b's. The production S → aA therefore yields strings with one more 'a' than 'b'. The productions SS and bSS preserve the property that the number of 'a's exceeds the number of 'b's by a positive integer, so the language is precisely the set of strings with at least one more 'a' than 'b'.
Incorrect. A correct characterization exists: the grammar generates exactly those strings with at least one more 'a' than 'b'. Therefore the choice that claims no description applies is false.

text:
Consider the context-free grammar G below. Here S is the starting non-terminal symbol, while a and b are terminal symbols.

The language generated by G is:
solution:
First, analyze the non-terminal T. The production rules are T → bT and T → b. This generates strings consisting of one or more 'b's. So, L(T) = { b^n | n ≥ 1 }.

Next, analyze the non-terminal S. The rules are S → aSb and S → T. The rule S → aSb allows us to add an 'a' at the beginning and a 'b' at the end of any string generated by S. If we apply this rule k times, we get a structure like a^k S b^k.

Finally, to terminate the recursion, we must use S → T. This replaces S with a string from L(T). Combining these, any string generated by S has the form a^k w b^k, where w ∈ L(T). Since w = b^n for some n ≥ 1, the total string is a^k b^n b^k = a^k b^{n+k}.

Let m = k be the number of 'a's and the total exponent of 'b' be N = n+k. Since n ≥ 1, we have N > k, which means the number of 'b's is strictly greater than the number of 'a's. Also, k can be 0 (if we go directly to T), so the number of 'a's can be 0. Therefore, the language is { am bn | 0 ≤ m < n }.

Which of the following is / are correct

I. A language is context free if and only if it is accepted by PDA

Correct Answer: C (Both I and II are true)

  • Statement II is true: Structurally, a PDA is formally defined as a finite automaton enhanced with an external, infinite memory storage known as a pushdown stack.

title: Which of the following CFGs cannot be simulated by an
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following CFGs cannot be simulated by an FSM?
solution:
To determine which CFG cannot be simulated by an FSM, we need to check whether the language generated by each CFG is regular or not. An FSM can only recognize regular languages. If a CFG generates a non-regular language, it cannot be simulated by an FSM.

Option A: S→Sa | b

This CFG generates strings of the form b, ba, baa, baaa, etc. This is equivalent to the regular expression b a*. Since this language is regular, it can be recognized by an FSM.

Option B: S→aSb | ab

This CFG generates strings of the form ab, aabb, aaabbb, etc. This is the language a^n b^n, which is not regular. It requires counting the number of a's and matching it with the number of b's, which cannot be done by an FSM. Therefore, this CFG cannot be simulated by an FSM.

Option C: S→abX, X→cY, Y→d | aX

This CFG generates strings starting with ab, followed by c, and then either d or a sequence of a's and c's. The structure is linear and does not require unbounded counting. The language is regular, so it can be recognized by an FSM.

Option D: S→Sb | a

This CFG generates strings of the form a, ab, abb, abbb, etc. This is equivalent to the regular expression a b*. Since this language is regular, it can be recognized by an FSM.

Option E: Question not attempted

This is not a valid CFG and does not represent a grammar. It is not a relevant choice for the question.

Therefore, the CFG that cannot be simulated by an FSM is Option B.

title: Consider the statements An unambiguous CFG will always generate DCFL.
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the statements

S1: An unambiguous CFG will always generate DCFL.

S2: A CFG for a DCFL will always be unambiguous.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE
solution:
Answer: Neither S1 nor S2.

Reasoning:

  • S1 is false. Example: the grammar S → 0S0 | 1S1 | ε generates the set of even-length palindromes over {0,1}. This grammar is unambiguous, but the language of palindromes is not a deterministic context-free language (a deterministic PDA cannot decide palindromes because it cannot deterministically find the midpoint and compare both halves). Thus an unambiguous CFG need not generate a DCFL.

  • S2 is false. Example: the language L = { a^n b^n | n ≥ 0 } is a deterministic CFL (there is a deterministic PDA that pushes a's and pops on b's). However, the following grammar generates the same language but is ambiguous:

    Grammar G:

    • S → a S b | T

    • T → a T b | ε

    Both S and T generate exactly the strings a^n b^n. For any n, a^n b^n can be derived either by expanding S using the S → a S b rule repeatedly or by using S → T and then expanding T. That gives two distinct parse trees for the same string, so the grammar is ambiguous even though the language is deterministic context-free. Hence having a CFG for a DCFL does not guarantee the CFG is unambiguous.

Conclusion: Both statements are false, so the correct choice is that neither S1 nor S2 is true.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Both statements are false. An unambiguous grammar can generate a non-deterministic CFL (example: the unambiguous grammar S → 0S0 | 1S1 | ε generates even-length palindromes, which are not deterministic CFLs). Conversely, a deterministic CFL can have an ambiguous grammar (see solution example), so having a CFG for a deterministic CFL does not guarantee the grammar is unambiguous.

Incorrect. Statement S1 is false: an unambiguous CFG can generate a language that is not a deterministic CFL (for example, even-length palindromes). Also S2 is false: a deterministic CFL may have an ambiguous grammar, so a CFG for a deterministic CFL need not be unambiguous. See full solution for examples.

Incorrect. Statement S2 is false because a deterministic CFL can have an ambiguous grammar (the solution gives an explicit ambiguous grammar for the deterministic language {a^n b^n}). Statement S1 is also false: an unambiguous grammar can generate a non-deterministic CFL (example: even-length palindromes).

Incorrect. Both statements are not true. S1 is false: an unambiguous CFG can generate languages that are not deterministic CFLs (example: even-length palindromes). S2 is false: a deterministic CFL can admit ambiguous grammars (example provided in the solution). The correct choice is that neither statement is true.

title: Which of the following are decidable? Whether the intersection of
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Which of the following are decidable?

I. Whether the intersection of two regular languages is finite

II. Whether a given context-free language is finite and hence regular.

III. Whether two push-down automata accept the same language

IV. Whether a given grammar is context-free

options.html: I and I I and I I and IV

solution:
Explanation:

Statement I: The intersection of two regular languages is regular (by closure property). Testing whether a regular language is finite is decidable. Therefore, statement I is decidable.

Statement II: The finiteness problem for context-free languages is decidable. Therefore, determining whether a given CFL is finite (and hence regular) is decidable.

Statement III: The equivalence problem for push-down automata (i.e., whether two PDAs accept the same language) is undecidable. Therefore, statement III is not decidable.

Statement IV: Checking whether a given grammar is context-free (i.e., whether it follows CFG rules) is decidable. Therefore, statement IV is decidable.

Thus, statements I, II, and IV are decidable, while III is not.

Step 1: Statement II is decidable (finiteness of CFL is decidable). Step 2: Statement III involves equivalence of two push-down automata, which is undecidable. Step 3: Since III is undecidable, this option is incorrect.

Step 3: Statement IV is decidable (checking if grammar is context-free is decidable). Step 4: This option includes all three decidable statements.

title: Which of the following is/are true?
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following is/are true?

options.html: A context free language L has 4 states in PDA. the complement of L has also 4 states in its PDA.
A context free language L has 4 states in DPDA. the complement of L has also 4 states in its DPDA.
Complement of a CFL language may be regular.
A DPDA has strictly less power compare to the NPDA.

solution:
Correct statements and explanations:

  • Statement: "A context free language L has 4 states in PDA. the complement of L has also 4 states in its PDA." — False. The complement of a context-free language need not be context-free, so there may be no PDA for the complement. Even when the complement is context-free, there is no general guarantee that a PDA for the complement will have the same number of states as the original.

  • Statement: "A context free language L has 4 states in DPDA. the complement of L has also 4 states in its DPDA." — Partly correct but misleading. Deterministic context-free languages (those accepted by a DPDA) are closed under complement, so the complement will be accepted by some DPDA. However, the exact number of states need not be preserved—there is no guarantee the DPDA for the complement will have the same number of states.

  • Statement: "Complement of a CFL language may be regular." — True. There exist CFLs whose complements are regular. For example, if the CFL is the empty language, its complement over the alphabet is Σ*, which is regular. So the complement may be regular (but need not be in general).

solution:
Closure properties tell us whether combining languages from a class using an operation (union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star) always yields another language of that same class. Regular languages (REG) are closed under union, intersection, and complement. Context-free languages (CFL) are closed under union, concatenation, and Kleene star — and, as an extended fact, a context-free language intersected with any regular language is always guaranteed to remain context-free, but this intersection is NOT guaranteed to be regular.

Checking each of the four statements against these closure facts:

  1. The intersection of a regular language and a context-free language is context-free — TRUE, directly from the closure property that a context-free language intersected with a regular language stays context-free.

  2. The intersection of a regular language and a context-free language is regular — this claims the stronger property of regularity, which closure only guarantees as context-freeness, not regularity.

  3. The union of two context-free languages is context-free — TRUE, since context-free languages are closed under union (their grammars/PDAs combine into one for the union).

  4. The union of two regular languages is regular — TRUE, since regular languages are closed under union (a product construction on their automata, or combining regular expressions, gives a single automaton/regex for the union).

Cross-check with a concrete counterexample: let R = Σ* (trivially regular) and L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}, a standard context-free language that is provably NOT regular (via the pumping lemma for regular languages). Then R ∩ L = L, which is context-free but not regular — directly disproving the claim that a regular-language/context-free-language intersection is always regular.

So the false statement is the one claiming that intersecting a regular language with a context-free language always gives a regular language.

title: The language accepted by the following Turing Machine is &LBA
subject: Theory of Computation
text: The language accepted by the following Turing Machine is
solution:
Language accepted: All strings consisting of one or more 0s followed by one or more 1s (i.e. {0^n1^m | n ≥ 1, m ≥ 1}).

  • Behavior of the start state (q0): on reading 0 it moves to the state that scans zeros; on reading 1 or blank it halts (reject). So the input must begin with at least one 0.

  • Behavior of the zero-scanning state (q1): it stays on 0s; on the first 1 it transitions to the one-scanning state; on blank it halts (reject). Thus there must be at least one 1 after the initial zeros.

  • Behavior of the one-scanning state (q2): it stays on 1s; if it encounters a 0 it halts (reject); when it sees the blank it moves to the final accepting state. Therefore no 0s are allowed after the first 1.

Example: Trace on the input 0011

  1. Start in q0; read first 0 -> move to q1.

  2. In q1; read next 0 -> stay in q1.

  3. In q1; read first 1 -> move to q2.

  4. In q2; read next 1 -> stay in q2.

  5. In q2; read blank -> go to qf (accept).

Conclusion: The machine accepts exactly those strings with one or more 0s followed by one or more 1s; it rejects strings that start with 1, contain no 1, or have any 0 after the first 1.

The statement "Accepts 0011" is true: the machine accepts 0011. Trace: q0 reads 0 -> q1; q1 reads 0 -> q1; q1 reads 1 -> q2; q2 reads 1 -> q2; q2 reads blank -> qf (accept). However, this single example is not a full description of the language. The general language is all strings of one or more 0s followed by one or more 1s.

This is incorrect. The machine does not accept strings where 0s and 1s alternate after the first 1 (i.e., it does not allow 0 after a 1). For example, 0101 alternates but is rejected when the machine sees a 0 after it has already moved to the state that reads only 1s.

This is incorrect. The machine does not accept all strings ending in 10. For instance, 10 starts with 1 and is immediately rejected by the initial state. The machine requires at least one leading 0 and then one or more 1s, with no 0s after the first 1.

title: The next move function of Turing machine is mapping &LBA
subject: Theory of Computation
text: The next move function δ of a Turing machine M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, B, F) is a mapping
solution:
Correct mapping: δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}

Explanation:

  • Domain Q × Γ: the function takes the current machine state (from Q) and the symbol currently under the tape head (from the tape alphabet Γ).

  • Codomain Q × Γ × {L, R}: the function returns the next state (in Q), the single symbol to write at the current tape cell (from Γ), and the head movement direction (left or right).

Notes on variants:

  • Using Γ* in the output (δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ* × {L, R}) corresponds to a generalized machine that can write a whole string in one step. This is not the standard single-step single-symbol write model.

  • Using Σ in the domain or output is incorrect because Σ is the input alphabet; the head reads and writes tape symbols from Γ (which includes Σ and the blank symbol).

  • For multi-tape machines the signature changes (e.g., δ: Q × Γ^k → Q × Γ^k × {L,S,R}^k), but for the usual single-tape deterministic Turing machine the correct and standard mapping is δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}.

optionFeedback.html: This mapping is incorrect because it uses the input alphabet Σ in the domain instead of the tape alphabet Γ, and it does not specify the head movement. The next-move function must read the current tape symbol (from Γ) and also indicate whether the head moves left or right.

This is nearly correct in form but incorrect in detail: it writes a symbol from the input alphabet Σ in the output rather than from the tape alphabet Γ. The correct single-tape deterministic Turing machine mapping writes a symbol from the tape alphabet Γ, not the input alphabet Σ.

This mapping incorrectly uses the input alphabet Σ in the domain. The next-move function must read the current tape symbol, which comes from the tape alphabet Γ. Using Σ in the domain makes the mapping invalid for the usual Turing machine model.

This mapping is a generalized form that allows writing an entire string (Γ*) in one move. The standard single-tape deterministic Turing machine uses a single tape-symbol write, so the usual definition is δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}. The Γ* version is valid only for a nonstandard or generalized machine that can overwrite multiple cells in one step; clarify which model is intended.

title: Question: Which of the following is/are true?
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Question:
Which of the following is/are true?

options.html: Finite automata with zero final states is possible.
If we make all the states of NFA as final, then it will accept all the substrings of the language.
If Mealy/Moore machine exists for a language, then the language is regular.
Turing machine with one final state is always possible.

solution:
Explanation of each statement:

  • "Finite automata with zero final states is possible." — True. A finite automaton can have no accepting states; such an automaton recognizes the empty language (it accepts no strings).

  • "If we make all the states of NFA as final, then it will accept all the substrings of the language." — False. Marking every state accepting makes the machine accept all prefixes of strings that reach those states. Substrings (contiguous parts that may start and end inside the string) are not generally accepted just by making states final.

  • "If Mealy/Moore machine exists for a language, then the language is regular." — False as stated. Mealy and Moore machines are finite-state transducers that map input sequences to output sequences. They are not acceptance devices by default. Only if a transducer is constructed to decide membership (outputting accept/reject) does that imply a corresponding finite automaton and hence regularity.

  • "Turing machine with one final state is always possible." — True. Any Turing machine with one or more accepting states can be transformed into an equivalent machine with a single accepting halting state by adding one new final state and redirecting the original accepting behaviors to transition to that single final state. This preserves the recognized language.

Conclusion: The true statements are the one about finite automata with zero final states and the one about converting to a Turing machine with a single final state.

optionFeedback.html: True. A finite automaton can have zero accepting (final) states. Such an automaton accepts the empty language (no string is accepted) because there is no state designated as accepting.

False. Making every state of an NFA accepting causes the machine to accept all prefixes of strings that lead to any reachable state, not all substrings. A substring can start in the middle of an input, but simply marking all states accepting does not ensure acceptance of arbitrary substrings.

False in the intended sense. Mealy and Moore machines are finite-state transducers that produce outputs for input sequences; they are not acceptance machines by default. The existence of a transducer for some input-output behavior does not by itself mean the set of accepted strings is a regular language unless the transducer is specifically used to decide membership.

True. Any Turing machine can be converted to an equivalent machine with a single accepting (final) state by adding one new final state and redirecting the original accepting behaviors to move to that single final state. This transformation preserves the recognized language.

title: Which of the following are false: &ClosureProperties
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following are false:

options.html: For two languages L1 and L2, If both are non regular then L1∩L2 is also non-regular.
Given encodings of 2 DFAs over the same set of alphabets, there is a TM which can tell whether or not they both accept same language or not.
The set of decidable languages is closed under the subset operation.
There exist a TM which can simulate the behaviour of any given TM on any given finite input

solution:
Summary: The false statements and explanations are given below.

  • Statement: For two languages L1 and L2, if both are non-regular then L1 ∩ L2 is also non-regular.

    Why this is false: Provide a counterexample. Let L1 = {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0} and L2 = {a^n b^{2n} | n ≥ 0}. Each language is non-regular, but their intersection is empty. The empty language is regular, so the intersection can be regular. Therefore the claim is false.

  • Statement: The set of decidable languages is closed under the subset operation.

    Why this is false: A decidable language can have undecidable subsets. For example, Σ* is decidable, but there exist undecidable subsets of Σ* (take any known undecidable language over the same alphabet). Hence decidability is not guaranteed for arbitrary subsets.

Other statements (true):

  • Given encodings of two DFAs over the same alphabet, there is a Turing machine that decides whether they accept the same language. Reason: construct the product automaton to accept the symmetric difference of the two languages and test emptiness by reachability; this procedure halts.

  • There exists a Turing machine that can simulate the behaviour of any given Turing machine on any given finite input. Reason: a universal Turing machine can read the encoding of any TM and its input and simulate its step-by-step execution.

optionFeedback.html: False. Counterexample: let L1 = {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0} and L2 = {a^n b^{2n} | n ≥ 0}. Both languages are non-regular, but their intersection is empty, and the empty language is regular. So the intersection need not be non-regular.

True. DFA equivalence is decidable. Construct the product automaton that accepts the symmetric difference of the two DFAs' languages; then check whether any accepting state is reachable (emptiness test). A Turing machine can perform these construction and reachability checks and halt with the correct answer.

False. A decidable language can have undecidable subsets. For example, Σ* is decidable, but there exist undecidable subsets of Σ* (take any known undecidable language over the same alphabet). Thus decidability is not preserved for arbitrary subsets.

True. A universal Turing machine exists: given the encoding of any Turing machine and a finite input, it can simulate that machine's computation on that input. Therefore such a TM can simulate the behaviour of any given TM on any given finite input.
