text:
Consider the following two languages, where ⟨M⟩ represents the encoding of a Turing Machine M:

L1​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that halts on all inputs w where w is a prime-length binary string}
L2​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that, on input ϵ (empty string), visits its initial state at least twice}
Which of the following statements accurately describes the decidability of L1​ and L2​?

options.html: L1​ is undecidable, but L2​ is decidable.
L1​ is decidable, but L2​ is undecidable.

solution:
This question tests your ability to distinguish between properties of a Turing Machine's language (which Rice's Theorem applies to) and properties of its computation (which Rice's Theorem does not apply to, and which must be analyzed directly, often via reduction).

Analysis of L₁

  • L1​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that halts on all inputs w where w is a prime-length binary string}

  • This language L1​ defines a property of the language L(M) accepted by the Turing Machine M. The property is "M halts on all strings w where ∣w∣ is prime."

  • We can check if this property is "non-trivial" to see if Rice's Theorem applies. A property is non-trivial if someTuring Machines (and their languages) have it, and some do not.

    1. TM that has the property: A simple TM Mhalt​ that halts on all inputs (e.g., it accepts Σ∗). This TM certainly halts on all prime-length strings.

    2. TM that does not have the property: A TM Mloop​ that is designed to loop forever only if the input string has a prime length (e.g., it loops on "10", length 2).

  • Since the property is non-trivial (it's not held by all TMs or by no TMs) and it is a property of the languageL(M), Rice's Theorem states that L1​ is undecidable.

Analysis of L₂

  • L2​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that, on input ϵ (empty string), visits its initial state at least twice}

  • This is a property of the TM's computation on a specific input (ϵ), not a property of the language L(M). Therefore, Rice's Theorem does not apply.

  • We must check for decidability by other means, typically by trying to reduce the Halting Problem to L2​.

  • Let's use the ϵ-Halting Problem (HALTϵ​), which is known to be undecidable. HALTϵ​={⟨M⟩∣M halts on input ϵ}.

  • We will construct a new TM M′ from an arbitrary TM M such that: M halts on ϵ⟺M′∈L2​

  • Construction of M′:

    • Let M have an initial state q0​.

    • Create M′ with a new, unique initial state qnew′​.

    • Define the transitions of M′ as follows:

      • On input ϵ, M′ starts in qnew′​. (This is Visit 1 to its initial state).

      • M′ immediately transitions to q0​ (the initial state of M) and begins simulating M on input ϵ.

      • Modify all "halting" transitions in M: If M would enter a halt state (qhalt​), M′ is programmed to instead transition back to qnew′​ and then halt.

  • Analyzing M′'s behavior:

    • Case 1: M halts on ϵ. M′ starts in qnew′​ (Visit 1), simulates M, and when M halts, M′ transitions back to qnew′​ (Visit 2). M′ then halts. In this case, M′ visits its initial state twice. Thus, M′∈L2​.

    • Case 2: M loops forever on ϵ. M′ starts in qnew′​ (Visit 1), simulates M, but the simulation never reaches M's halt state. Since qnew′​ is a new state not in M, the simulation will never re-enter qnew′​. M′ only visits its initial state once. Thus, M′∈/L2​.

  • Since we have successfully created a reduction from the undecidable HALTϵ​ problem to L2​, L2​ must also be undecidable.

Conclusion:

  • L1​ is undecidable (by Rice's Theorem).

  • L2​ is undecidable (by reduction from the Halting Problem).

Therefore, both languages are undecidable.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The first language is undecidable: it expresses a nontrivial semantic property of the machine's computed partial function (whether the machine halts on every prime-length input), so Rice-style undecidability applies. The second language is also undecidable: one can reduce the halting-on-empty-string problem to it by building a machine that returns to a new start state exactly when the original machine halts.

Incorrect. While the first language is indeed undecidable (it is a nontrivial semantic property of the machine's behavior, so Rice-style reasoning applies), the second language is not decidable. Reduce the halting-on-empty-string problem to the second language by creating a machine that revisits a new initial state iff the original machine halts on the empty input; this shows the second language is undecidable.

Incorrect. The second language being undecidable is correct, but the first language is not decidable. The property "halts on all prime-length inputs" is a nontrivial semantic property of the machine's computed partial function, so Rice-style undecidability applies to the first language as well.

Correct. Both languages are undecidable. The first is undecidable because it expresses a nontrivial semantic property of the machine's computed function (Rice-style undecidability). The second is undecidable because you can reduce the halting-on-empty-string problem to it by constructing a machine that returns to a new initial state exactly when the original machine halts on the empty input.

title: Consider the languages: L1​={⟨M⟩∣M is TM that accepts where ∣w∣≤2025}L2​={⟨M⟩∣M
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the languages:

L1​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that accepts w where ∣w∣≤2025}
L2​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that accepts w where ∣w∣≥2025}

Which of the following statements is correct regarding the decidability of L1​ and L2​?

options.html: L1​ is undecidable, but L2​ is decidable
L1​ is decidable, but L2​ is undecidable

solution:
This is a subtle application of Rice's Theorem. Rice's Theorem states that any non-trivial property of the language recognized by a Turing Machine is undecidable. A "non-trivial" property is one that some RE languages have and others do not.

For L1​: The property is "Does the TM accept at least one string of length ≤2025?". This is a non-trivial property of the language L(M). The empty language ∅ does not have this property, but the language {a} does. By Rice's Theorem, L1​ is undecidable.

For L2​: The property is "Does the TM accept at least one string of length ≥2025?". This is also a non-trivial property. The empty language ∅ does not have it, but the language Σ∗ (accepting all strings) does. By Rice's Theorem, L2​ is also undecidable.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Neither property is decidable. Both questions ask whether the language recognized by the machine contains some string meeting a length constraint, which is a nontrivial semantic property of the recognized language. By Rice's Theorem such nontrivial properties are undecidable. (You can semidecide each property by searching for an accepting input, but you cannot always decide it.)

Incorrect. The claim that the second language is decidable is wrong. The property 'the language contains some string of length at least 2025' is a nontrivial property of the language recognized by the machine, so Rice's Theorem implies it is undecidable. Both languages are undecidable for the same general reason.

Incorrect. The claim that the first language is decidable is incorrect. Although there are only finitely many candidate strings of length ≤2025, a Turing machine may loop on some of them, so you cannot in general decide whether any of those finite inputs is accepted. This is a nontrivial semantic property, so Rice's Theorem implies undecidability.

Correct. Both languages ask whether the machine's recognized language contains at least one string meeting a length constraint; these are nontrivial properties of the language. Rice's Theorem implies both are undecidable. Note: both properties are semidecidable (you can search for an accepting input), but they are not decidable in general.

title: Which of the following is True?
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following is True?

options.html: Every subset of NOT RE is countable.
Every infinite regular language has RE (Undecidable) or NOT REC language as subset.
There are subsets of NOT RE which are decidable.
Union of countable set and uncountable set is always uncountable.

solution:
Answer: The true statements are:

  • Every infinite regular language has RE (Undecidable) or NOT REC language as subset.

  • Union of countable set and uncountable set is always uncountable.

Brief explanations for each given statement:

  • Every subset of NOT RE is countable: False. The collection of non-RE languages is uncountable (there are uncountably many languages overall but only countably many RE languages), so it has uncountable subsets (for example, the whole non-RE collection).

  • Every infinite regular language has RE (Undecidable) or NOT REC language as subset: True. Any infinite regular language L can be enumerated computably, yielding a computable bijection f: N → L. For any subset S of N, f(S) is a subset of L. Taking S to be a known RE-undecidable set (e.g., the halting set) gives an RE undecidable subset of L; taking S to be a known non-RE subset of N gives a non-RE subset of L.

  • There are subsets of NOT RE which are decidable: False. Any decidable (recursive) language is recursively enumerable, so it cannot belong to the collection of non-RE languages. Thus there are no decidable languages inside NOT RE.

  • Union of countable set and uncountable set is always uncountable: True. If one set is uncountable, the union with any countable set still contains the uncountable set as a subset, so the union is uncountable (its cardinality cannot decrease).

optionFeedback.html: False. The collection of languages that are not recursively enumerable is itself uncountable, so it has uncountable subsets. In particular, the set of all non-RE languages is an uncountable subset, so it is not true that every subset of the non-RE collection is countable. (There are uncountably many languages over any nontrivial alphabet, while RE is only countable.)

True. If L is any infinite regular language, one can computably enumerate its elements and build a computable bijection f: N → L. For any subset S ⊆ N, the image f(S) is a subset of L. Choosing S to be a known RE but undecidable set (for example the halting set) yields an RE undecidable subset of L; choosing S to be a known non-RE subset of N yields a non-RE subset of L. Thus every infinite regular language contains both kinds of subsets.

False. Any decidable (recursive) language is, by definition, recursively enumerable. Therefore a decidable language cannot be an element of the collection of non-RE languages. So there are no decidable languages inside the non-RE collection.

True. If one set is uncountable, adding any countable set cannot reduce cardinality: the union contains the uncountable set as a subset, so the union is uncountable. For example, the union of the real numbers (uncountable) with the prime numbers (countable) is uncountable.

title: Which of the following are Decidable? {<TM> L(TM) is RE}
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Which of the following are Decidable?

L1 = {<TM> | L(TM) is RE}

L2 = {<TM> | L(TM) has exactly 2025 members}

L3 = {<TM> | M makes different and unique numbers of steps on all inputs}

L4 = {<TM> | L(TM) is non-empty}

L5 = {<TM> | L(TM) is CFL but not DCFL}
solution:
Summary: Only the property that a machine's language is recursively enumerable is decidable (it is true for every Turing machine). The other listed properties are undecidable. Since none of the provided answer choices lists only that decidable language, the choice that says "none" is the correct selection among the given options.

Details by language:

  • L1 = {⟨TM⟩ | L(TM) is RE}: Decidable. Reason: For any Turing machine M, the set L(M) is, by definition, recursively enumerable (it is exactly the language recognized by M). Thus the predicate "L(M) is RE" holds for every encoding ⟨M⟩, so the language of encodings is the set of all encodings and can be decided trivially (always accept).

  • L2 = {⟨TM⟩ | L(TM) has exactly 2025 members}: Undecidable. Sketch of reduction: Given an instance (M,w) of the acceptance problem, construct a machine M' that on any input x first ignores x, simulates M on w, and if M accepts w then accepts exactly a fixed set of 2025 distinct strings (e.g., a fixed 2025-member set); otherwise M' accepts nothing. Then L(M') has size 2025 iff M accepts w. Deciding the 2025-size property would decide acceptance, so it is undecidable.

  • L3 = {⟨TM⟩ | M makes different and unique numbers of steps on all inputs}: Undecidable. Sketch: The property compares halting times across inputs, so one can encode halting/acceptance information into the runtimes on specially chosen inputs. Any algorithm deciding the uniqueness-of-runtime property would resolve halting/acceptance instances; hence it is undecidable.

  • L4 = {⟨TM⟩ | L(TM) is non-empty}: Undecidable. Sketch: Reduce from the acceptance problem. Given (M,w), build M' that on any input simulates M on w and accepts iff M accepts w. Then L(M') is non-empty iff M accepts w. Thus non-emptiness is undecidable.

  • L5 = {⟨TM⟩ | L(TM) is CFL but not DCFL}: Undecidable. Reason: Being a context-free language (or being context-free but not deterministic context-free) is a nontrivial semantic property of the language recognized by a Turing machine. By Rice's theorem (properties of the language recognized by a TM that are nontrivial are undecidable), this decision problem is undecidable.

Conclusion: Only the property in L1 is decidable (it is always true). The other properties L2, L3, L4, and L5 are undecidable. Because none of the provided answer-choices lists exactly that single decidable language, the offered choice that states "none" (i.e., none of the other answer-sets is correct) is the correct selection among the given choices.

optionFeedback.html: This choice asserts that the languages 'L1, L2, L3' are decidable. That is incorrect. The statement 'L1 is RE' holds for every Turing machine by definition (the language recognized by a Turing machine is recursively enumerable), so the decision problem asking whether a given TM's language is RE is trivial (always true) and thus decidable. However, deciding whether a TM's language has exactly 2025 strings or whether the TM runs in pairwise distinct numbers of steps on all inputs are undecidable problems (they can be used to encode halting/acceptance behavior). Because two of the three listed languages are undecidable, this choice is wrong.

This choice claims only the languages 'L4' and 'L5' are decidable. That is incorrect. The non-emptiness problem for Turing machines (deciding whether a TM's language is non-empty) is undecidable by a standard reduction from the halting/acceptance problem. Determining whether a TM's language is context-free but not deterministic context-free is also undecidable (this is a nontrivial semantic property of the TM's language and falls under Rice-style arguments). Moreover, the language 'L1' (asking whether the TM's language is RE) is trivially true for every TM and therefore decidable, so excluding it makes this choice wrong.

This choice claims only 'L5' is decidable. That is incorrect. The property 'L(TM) is CFL but not DCFL' is undecidable: it is a nontrivial property of the language recognized by a TM, so deciding it is undecidable via Rice-style reasoning. Also, 'L1' is decidable (trivially true for every TM), so the correct decidable set is not just L5. Therefore this choice is wrong.

This choice says 'none' (meaning none of the other listed answer-sets is correct). That is the correct selection among the provided options because the only decidable language among L1–L5 is the one asking whether L(TM) is recursively enumerable, which is always true for any TM and thus decidable; none of the other provided answer-sets lists just that language. The other problems — whether a TM's language has exactly 2025 members, whether the TM has distinct halting times on all inputs, whether the TM's language is non-empty, and whether the TM's language is CFL but not DCFL — are undecidable (sketches: use simple reductions from acceptance/halting and Rice-style arguments).

title: Which of the following are True? &ClosureProperties
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following are True?

options.html: Does the given program ever produce an output is undecidable.
State entry problem of Turing machine is undecidable.
Membership problem of unrestricted grammar is polynomial-time reducible to halting problem of Turing machine.
Undecidable problems are those for which we can't construct Turing machines.

solution:
Final answer: the following three statements are true: "Does the given program ever produce an output is undecidable."; "State entry problem of Turing machine is undecidable."; and "Membership problem of unrestricted grammar is polynomial-time reducible to halting problem of Turing machine.". The statement "Undecidable problems are those for which we can't construct Turing machines." is false.

  • Does the given program ever produce an output is undecidable: Constructive reason: given an instance (M, w) of the halting problem, build a program that simulates M on w and prints output if and only if M halts. If we could decide whether that program ever produces output, we would decide halting. Hence the problem is undecidable.

  • State entry problem of a Turing machine is undecidable: Explanation: given a machine and input, asking whether the machine ever enters a particular state q is undecidable because one can reduce the halting problem to it by designing a machine that enters q exactly when a simulated machine halts.

  • Membership problem of unrestricted grammar reduces to the halting problem: Reason: given an unrestricted (type-0) grammar G and a string w, one can construct a Turing machine that enumerates all derivations of G and halts when it finds a derivation that produces w. Thus w is in L(G) if and only if the constructed machine halts. This gives a computable (and with standard encodings, implementable in polynomial time) reduction to the halting problem.

  • Incorrect characterization of undecidable problems: Clarification: undecidable means there is no Turing machine that always halts and correctly decides membership for every input. It does not mean no Turing machine can be built at all. Many undecidable problems are semi-decidable (recursively enumerable): there exists a Turing machine that accepts yes-instances and may run forever on no-instances (for example, the halting problem is semidecidable but not decidable).

Answer summary: the first three statements are true; the last statement is false.

optionFeedback.html: True. Determining whether a given program ever produces any output is undecidable because it can encode the halting problem. From an instance (M, w) of the halting problem you can build a program that simulates M on w and prints something if and only if M halts; deciding ‘‘ever produce output’’ for that program would decide halting.

True. The state entry problem (given a Turing machine M, input w, and state q: will M ever enter state q on input w?) is undecidable. One reduces the halting problem to it by constructing a machine that enters q exactly when a simulated machine halts, so a decider for state entry would decide halting.

True. Membership for unrestricted (type-0) grammars is recursively enumerable and reduces to the halting problem. Given a grammar G and word w, construct a Turing machine that systematically enumerates derivations of G and halts if it finds a derivation for w; then w ∈ L(G) iff the constructed machine halts. The reduction is computable and, with standard encodings, can be implemented efficiently.

False. ‘‘Undecidable’’ means there is no Turing machine that always halts and correctly decides membership for every input. It does not mean no Turing machine can be constructed at all. Many undecidable problems are semi-decidable (recursively enumerable): there exists a Turing machine that accepts all yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances (for example, the halting problem is undecidable but semidecidable).

title: Which of the following is/are Undecidable? &ClosureProperties
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following is/are Undecidable?

options.html: Does L(M) contain any two strings of the same length where L(M) is the language of Turing machine M.
Does L(TM) contain a string of length k for some given k ≥ 1.

solution:
Answer: All four problems are undecidable.

  • Does L(M) contain any two strings of the same length? Reason (Rice's theorem): This property depends only on the language recognized by the Turing machine and is nontrivial (some r.e. languages have two strings of the same length, some do not). By Rice's theorem any nontrivial property of TM-recognizable languages is undecidable.

  • Does L(TM) contain a string of length k for some given k ≥ 1? Reason (Rice's theorem and semi-decidability): For a given k the property 'language contains a string of length k' is a nontrivial property of the language, so Rice's theorem implies undecidability. The problem is, however, recursively enumerable: enumerate all strings of length k and simulate the machine on each in dovetailing; if any accept you will eventually find one. There is no general procedure that always decides the 'no' case, so the problem is not decidable in general.

  • Blank tape problem. Reason (reduction from Halting): Given an instance <M,w> of the halting problem, construct a machine M' that on its blank input writes an encoding of w and simulates M on w; if M halts on w then M' erases its tape and halts leaving the tape blank. Thus M halts on w iff M' can halt with a blank tape. Deciding the blank tape property would decide halting, so the blank tape problem is undecidable.

  • L = {⟨PDA⟩ | PDA accepts Σ*}. Reason (universality for PDAs/CFGs): Deciding whether a pushdown automaton (or equivalent context-free grammar) accepts all strings over the alphabet is the universality problem for context-free languages, which is known to be undecidable by standard reductions (for example from Post's Correspondence Problem or other undecidable problems).

optionFeedback.html: This property is undecidable. It depends only on the language recognized by the Turing machine (not on the machine encoding) and is nontrivial (some recursively enumerable languages have two strings of the same length, others do not). By Rice's theorem any nontrivial property of the language of a Turing machine is undecidable.

Undecidable in general. For a given k the property 'there exists an accepted string of length k' is a nontrivial property of the language, so Rice's theorem implies undecidability. Note: the problem is semi-decidable (recursively enumerable): enumerate all strings of length k and simulate the machine on them in dovetailed fashion — if any simulation accepts you will eventually find it — but there is no general procedure to always decide the 'no' case.

Undecidable. The blank tape problem can be shown undecidable by reduction from the halting problem: given a machine and input, construct a new machine that simulates the given machine and, if it halts, erases its tape and halts with a blank tape. Thus deciding the blank tape property would decide halting.

Undecidable. The universality problem for pushdown automata (equivalently for context-free grammars) — deciding whether the PDA accepts every string over the alphabet — is a standard undecidable problem. There are well-known reductions (e.g., from PCP or other undecidable problems) that prove universality for CFGs/PDAs is undecidable.

text:
Consider the following languages

L1={ | M is a TM such that M does not change the input symbols on the tape}

L2={ | M is a TM such that M does not change any symbol on the tape}

Select the correct option.

options.html: Both L1 and L2 are recursive
L1 is recursive and L2 is recursively enumerable but not recursive
L2 is recursive and L1 is recursively enumerable but not recursive
Both L1 and L2 are recursively enumerable but not recursive

solution:
Explanation:

L1 is undecidable as it is equivalent to halting problem of TM, suppose we have a TM M1 for L1, and suppose we given input <M> to M1 and M1 run this with some string "w", Now whenever M try to modify any symbol on "w" then M1 will halt by rejecting <M>. If M halts on "w" without doing any change in "w" then M1 will accept <M>, but suppose if M goes to infinite loop then M1 will also go to infinite loop. Hence M1 is TM which give guarantee only in case of string acceptance so L1 corresponds to rec enum language (hence undecidable)

L2 = { ⟨M⟩ | M does not change any symbol on the tape }

The machine:

Cannot write anything at all

Must behave like a read-only TM

This is a syntactic restriction—we can check the transition function and verify:

No transition writes a symbol different from what it reads.

L2 is Decidable

We can:

Inspect the transition function of M

Check whether every transition satisfies:

write symbol = read symbol

This is a finite, mechanical check → Decidable

optionFeedback.html: L1 describes a non-trivial property of Turing Machines, which is undecidable by Rice's Theorem. Thus, L1 cannot be recursive.
L1 involves a semantic property of TMs that is undecidable, so the claim that L1 is recursive is incorrect.
L2 is decidable since its definition relies on the transition function syntax. L1 concerns semantic behavior across all inputs, rendering it undecidable while remaining recursively enumerable.
L2 is actually decidable. Checking if a TM changes any symbol can be done by inspecting its transition function, making it recursive.

title: Consider the following problem “Given Turing Machine over the input
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the following problem X

“Given a Turing Machine M over the input alphabet Σ any state q of M and word Σ*, does the computation of M on w visit the state q”

Which of the following X is correct?

options.html: X is undecidable but not even partially decidable

solution: The State-Entry Problem X asks if a Turing Machine M ever visits a specific state q on input w. It is undecidable because solving it would easily solve the Halting Problem (by making the halting state q). However, it is partially decidable (recursively enumerable) because we can simulate M on w; if it ever enters state q, we can halt and answer "yes". Thus, Option A is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Rice's theorem or reduction from the Halting Problem proves it is undecidable. It is partially decidable (recursively enumerable) because a standard Turing Machine simulator can eventually detect if state q is visited.
Incorrect. The problem asks a "yes" or "no" question ("does the computation... visit the state q"), which is the exact definition of a decision problem.

Incorrect. If a general algorithm existed to determine whether any state q is reached, we could use it to decide if a machine halts by designating the halting state as q. Since the Halting Problem is undecidable, this is also undecidable.

Incorrect. While it is undecidable, it is semi-decidable (partially decidable). A TM can accept if the answer is "yes" by simply running the computation, though it may loop infinitely if the answer is "no".

title: Which of the following is decidable
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following is decidable ?
solution: The equivalence problem for Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs) is decidable. Unlike Turing Machines, where problems like Halting and Equivalence are undecidable, DFAs have finite states allowing standard algorithms to determine equivalence.

optionFeedback.html: The Halting Problem for Turing Machines is a classic undecidable problem.
EMPTINESS PROBLEM of TM is also undecidable.
EQUIVALENCE OF DFA is decidable because you can construct a new DFA that accepts the symmetric difference of two DFAs. If this resulting language is empty, the original DFAs are equivalent.
EQUIVALENCE OF TM is undecidable. Unlike DFAs, determining if two Turing Machines accept the same language cannot be algorithmically decided.

title: Which of the following problems is undecidable
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following problems is undecidable ?
solution: The Halting problem for Turing machines is undecidable because no algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary program will halt on a given input. This was proven by Alan Turing in 1936 using diagonalization arguments.

optionFeedback.html: This option is incorrect because the membership problem for regular languages is decidable. You should check if you are confusing regular language properties with undecidable problems like the halting problem.

The Halting problem for Turing machines is undecidable because no algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary program will halt on a given input. This was proven by Alan Turing in 1936 using diagonalization arguments.
The emptiness problem for finite automata is decidable. You can check if a DFA accepts any string by testing reachability of an accepting state from the start state using graph traversal algorithms.
The Equivalence problem for DFAs is decidable

title: Which of the following conversion is not possible (algorithmically)?
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following conversion is not possible (algorithmically)?

options.html: Non-deterministic pushdown automata to deterministic pushdown automata
Non-deterministic finite state automata to deterministic finite state automata
Non-deterministic Turing machine to deterministic Turing machine

solution:
Step 1: Regular grammar to context-free grammar – Every regular grammar is a context-free grammar. Therefore, this conversion is always possible algorithmically.

Step 2: Non-deterministic pushdown automata to deterministic pushdown automata – Not all languages accepted by NPDA can be accepted by DPDA. Hence, this conversion is not always possible algorithmically.

Step 3: Non-deterministic finite state automata to deterministic finite state automata – The subset construction algorithm converts any NFA to an equivalent DFA. This is always possible algorithmically.

Step 4: Non-deterministic Turing machine to deterministic Turing machine – Any NTM can be simulated by a DTM using a breadth-first search of computation paths. This conversion is algorithmically possible.

title: What is the computational complexity of the halting problem? Halting
subject: Theory of Computation
text: What is the computational complexity of the halting problem?
solution:
The halting problem asks whether a given program will halt on a given input. It was proven by Alan Turing that no algorithm can solve this problem for all possible program-input pairs. This means the problem is undecidable, or not computable. Therefore, the computational complexity is not expressible in standard time complexity classes like O(1) or O(n), as no algorithm exists to compute the answer in finite time.

title: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding Recursive and
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding Recursive (R) and Recursively Enumerable (RE) languages?

options.html: The union of two Recursively Enumerable (RE) languages is always Recursively Enumerable.

The complement of a Recursive language is always Recursive.
The complement of a Recursively Enumerable (RE) language is always Recursively Enumerable.

solution:
This question tests your knowledge of the closure properties of Recursive and RE languages.

(A) Union of RE is RE: This is TRUE. If L1​ and L2​ are RE, they are accepted by Turing Machines M1​ and M2​respectively. We can construct a new TM Munion​ that, on input w, simulates M1​ and M2​ in parallel (e.g., by alternating steps). If either M1​ or M2​ accepts, Munion​ accepts. This new TM accepts the union L1​∪L2​.
(B) L is R iff L and LC are RE: This is TRUE. This is the standard theorem defining Recursive languages in terms of RE languages.
If L is R, it's accepted by a total TM M that always halts. L is clearly RE. Its complement LC is also accepted by a total TM M′ (that just flips M's accept/reject states), so LC is also R, and thus RE.
If L and LC are both RE, we have TMs M1​ (for L) and M2​ (for LC). We can run them in parallel on an input w. Since w must be in either L or LC, one of M1​ or M2​ is guaranteed to halt and accept. If M1​accepts, we accept. If M2​ accepts, we reject. This creates a total TM, proving L is Recursive.

(C) Complement of R is R: This is TRUE. As explained in (B), if L is Recursive, it has a total TM M that always halts. A TM M′ for LC can be built by simply swapping the accept and reject states of M. M′ will also always halt, making LC Recursive.
(D) Complement of RE is RE: This is FALSE. This is the key distinction. The set of RE languages is not closed under complementation. If this statement were true, it would imply that for any RE language L, its complement LC is also RE. By the theorem in (B), this would mean every RE language is also Recursive. This is false; the Halting Problem is a well-known example of a language that is RE but not Recursive. Therefore, the complement of an RE language is not guaranteed to be RE.

Conversely, if both a language and its complement are RE, run their acceptors in dovetailed fashion on an input; one will eventually accept, allowing you to decide membership, so the language is Recursive.

title: Which of the following statements is False? &LBA
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following statements is False?

options.html: Pumping lemma is necessary and sufficient to prove language is regular.
Any language L(M), that is accepted by NTM, is always Turing recognizable.
Union of two or more uncountable sets is always uncountable.

solution:
Correct false statements: "Pumping lemma is necessary and sufficient to prove language is regular." and "Every superset of RE is decidable."

  • Pumping lemma statement: The pumping lemma gives a necessary property that every regular language satisfies. It is used mainly to prove non-regularity by showing a language fails this property.

    Why the statement is false: Satisfying the pumping lemma conditions does not guarantee a language is regular, so the lemma is not sufficient. To prove regularity, construct a finite automaton or a regular expression, or use Myhill–Nerode.

  • NTM acceptance statement: A language accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine is Turing-recognizable (recursively enumerable).

    Why this is true: You can simulate nondeterministic computation by interleaving (dovetailing) all nondeterministic branches; if any branch accepts, the simulation eventually accepts, so the language is recognizable.

  • Superset of RE statement: "Every superset of RE is decidable."

    Why the statement is false: Take the empty language, which is recursively enumerable. There exist supersets of the empty language that are undecidable (for example, the halting problem language contains the empty set and is undecidable). Therefore, being a superset of an RE language does not ensure decidability.

  • Union of uncountable sets statement: The union of two or more uncountable sets is uncountable.

    Why this is true: If at least one set in the union is uncountable, the union contains that uncountable set and hence is uncountable.

Summary: The two false statements are the pumping lemma sufficiency claim and the claim that every superset of an RE language is decidable. The other two statements are correct with the reasons above.

title: Which of following problems are undecidable? Membership problem in context-free
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Which of following problems are undecidable?

I. Membership problem in context-free languages
II. Whether a given context-free language is regular
III. Whether a finite state automaton halts on all inputs
IV. Membership problem for type 0 languages
solution:
Correct Answer: D (II and IV)

  • II is Undecidable: Checking if a context-free language is regular is a well-known undecidable problem (proven via Rice's Theorem or reduction from the Post Correspondence Problem).

  • IV is Undecidable: Type 0 languages are Recursively Enumerable (RE). The membership problem for $RE$ languages is equivalent to the Halting Problem, which is undecidable.

  • I & III are Decidable: Membership for CFLs is decidable (CYK algorithm). A Finite State Automaton (DFA/NFA) always halts on all inputs because it processes exactly one input symbol per transition and has no infinite loops without consuming input; hence, its halting problem is trivially decidable.

solution:
Two closure results govern this question: recursive languages are closed under complement, and a recursively enumerable (r.e.) language intersected with a recursive language is again r.e.; separately, the set of all Turing machines is countable because each machine has a finite description over a finite alphabet.

  • Recursive (decidable) languages are closed under complement: if L₁ is recursive, its complement L₁′ is also recursive.

  • An r.e. language intersected with a recursive language is r.e.: to recognize membership in the intersection, first run the recursive language's decider, which always halts; only if it accepts do you run the r.e. language's semi-decision procedure — the overall procedure need not halt when the input is not in the intersection, which is exactly what recursive enumerability requires.

  • Every Turing machine has a finite transition-table description over a finite alphabet, so it can be written as a finite binary string; the set of all finite binary strings is countably infinite.

Applying this to the two statements:

  1. S₁: L₁ is recursive, so its complement L₁′ is recursive. L₂ − L₁ = L₂ ∩ L₁′. Since L₂ is r.e. and L₁′ is recursive, this intersection is r.e. — S₁ holds.

  2. S₂: Each Turing machine's description (states, transitions, tape alphabet) is a finite string over a finite alphabet. Enumerating all finite strings by length gives a bijection with a subset of ℕ, so the set of all Turing machines is countable — S₂ holds.

  3. Both statements are true, so the correct choice is 'Both S₁ and S₂ are correct.'

The closure-under-complement and r.e.-intersect-recursive results are standard theorems, independent of this specific L₁, L₂ — so S₁ holds for any such pair, not just this one. For S₂, contrast with the (uncountable) set of all possible languages over an alphabet: that larger set is uncountable, which is exactly why not every language is decidable or recognizable — but the machines themselves, being finite descriptions, remain countable.

title: Which of the following sets is/are uncountable? &LBA
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following sets is/are uncountable?

options.html: Set of all languages except RE is countable
Set of all RE ∪ set of all CFL ∪ set of all regular languages

solution:
Key facts:

  • The set Σ* of all finite strings is countable.

  • The set of all languages over Σ is 2^{Σ*} (the power set of Σ*), which is uncountable (Cantor diagonalization).

  • Recursively enumerable (RE) languages are countable because Turing machines (or their encodings) can be enumerated.

  • Context-free languages (CFL) and regular languages are also countable (grammars, automata, or their encodings can be enumerated).

Consequences:

  • The set described as "set of all languages except RE" (all languages that are not recursively enumerable) is uncountable because 2^{Σ*} is uncountable and removing the countable set RE leaves an uncountable set.

  • The set described as "set of all not RE languages" is the same set and therefore uncountable for the same reason.

  • The set described as "set of all non-regular languages" is uncountable because the regular languages are countable, so their complement in 2^{Σ*} is uncountable.

  • The set described as the union "RE ∪ CFL ∪ regular languages" is countable, since it is a union of countable sets and a countable union of countable sets is countable.

Final summary: the three descriptions that denote complements of countable classes inside the full power set (the first three listed items) are uncountable; the union of RE, CFL and regular languages is countable.

optionFeedback.html: The set described as "set of all languages except RE" (i.e., all languages that are not recursively enumerable) is uncountable. Reason: the set of all languages over an alphabet is the power set 2^{Σ*}, which is uncountable by Cantor diagonalization, while the set of RE languages is countable (machines/programs can be enumerated). Removing a countable subset from an uncountable set leaves it uncountable, so the set of all languages except RE is uncountable. The statement claiming it is countable is incorrect.

The set described as "set of all not RE languages" (all languages that are not recursively enumerable) is uncountable. Explanation: 2^{Σ*} is uncountable and the class of RE languages is countable, so their complement in 2^{Σ*} is uncountable. Emphasize that "not RE" means complement of RE within all languages, which is uncountable.

The set described as "set of all non-regular languages" is uncountable. Reason: the set of all regular languages is countable (finite automata or regular expressions can be encoded and enumerated), while the set of all languages 2^{Σ*} is uncountable; therefore the complement (non-regular languages) is uncountable.

The set described as "set of all RE ∪ set of all CFL ∪ set of all regular languages" is countable. Reason: recursively enumerable languages are countable, context-free languages are countable, and regular languages are countable. A countable union of countable sets is countable, so the union remains countable.

title: Consider the language: is Turing machine} L(M) Complement of {⟨ww⟩
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Consider the language:
L1 = {⟨M⟩ ∣ M is a Turing machine}
L(M) ≤p Complement of {⟨ww⟩ ∣ w∈(a,b)*}
Then L1​ is:
solution:
Interpretation: L1 = {⟨M⟩ | L(M) ⊆ complement({ww | w ∈ {a,b}*}) }.

Key facts:

  • {ww} is decidable. Given an input x, we can check all possible splits (in particular check if its length is even and the two halves are equal), so membership in {ww} is decidable.

  • Hence the complement of {ww} is also decidable and is a nontrivial subset of Σ* (neither empty nor all strings).

Undecidability (Rice's theorem): The property 'L(M) is a subset of this fixed nontrivial decidable set' depends only on the language recognized by M and is nontrivial (some languages satisfy it, some do not). By Rice's theorem, any nontrivial property of the language recognized by Turing machines is undecidable. Therefore membership in L1 is undecidable.

Membership in co-RE:

  • Look at the complement of L1: it consists of all ⟨M⟩ for which there exists a string x with x ∈ L(M) and x ∈ {ww}.

  • To semidecide the complement, enumerate candidate x, decide whether x ∈ {ww} (possible since {ww} is decidable), and simulate M on x; if M accepts and x ∈ {ww}, accept ⟨M⟩. Thus the complement is recursively enumerable.

Conclusion: L1 is undecidable. Its complement is recursively enumerable, so L1 is in co-RE (but not r.e. in general). The original solution claiming decidability is incorrect.

Incorrect. The complement of this set is recursively enumerable: there exists an input x in {ww} that the machine accepts, and we can enumerate such witnesses. Therefore the original language is (in general) in co-RE, not RE.

Incorrect. This language is not decidable. By Rice's theorem the property 'the language of M is a subset of a fixed nontrivial decidable set' is a nontrivial language property of Turing machines and hence undecidable. However, its complement is r.e., so the language is co-r.e. (not decidable in general).

Incorrect. The given information is sufficient: {ww} is a decidable set, and from that we can determine that the property 'L(M) is contained in the complement of {ww}' is undecidable but its complement is r.e. So the correct classification is 'undecidable (co-RE)', not 'data insufficient'.

title: If and is undecidable, then what about Find the true
subject: Theory of Computation
text: If L1 ≤P L2​ and L2 is undecidable, then what about L1​? Find the true statement:

options.html: L1​ may or may not be decidable

solution:
Key idea: If there is a polynomial-time (or many-one) reduction f with x ∈ L1 iff f(x) ∈ L2, then a decider for L2 composed with f would decide L1. Thus if L2 were decidable, L1 must be decidable. However, the fact that L2 is undecidable does not force any particular status for L1.

  • Example where L1 is decidable:

    Let L1 = ∅ (decidable). Since L2 is undecidable it cannot be Σ*, so there exists some fixed string s0 not in L2. Define f(x)=s0 for all x. Then x ∈ L1 is always false and f(x) ∈ L2 is always false, so x ∈ L1 iff f(x) ∈ L2 holds. Thus L1 reduces to L2 even though L1 is decidable.

  • Example where L1 is undecidable:

    Take L1 = L2 (or any known undecidable language that reduces to L2). The identity reduction shows L1 can be undecidable.

Answer: Therefore, L1 may or may not be decidable. Reducibility to an undecidable language does not determine L1's decidability in general.

optionFeedback.html: This is incorrect. It is possible for L1 to be decidable even though L2 is undecidable. For example, the empty language (which is decidable) can be reduced to many undecidable languages by mapping every input to a fixed string not in L2, so reducibility does not prevent L1 from being decidable.

This is incorrect. Reducibility from L1 to an undecidable L2 does not force L1 to be undecidable. For instance, L1 could be decidable (see example with the empty language). Conversely, if L1 equals L2, L1 can be undecidable — so both possibilities occur.

Correct. If L1 reduces to L2 and L2 is undecidable, no definite conclusion follows about L1: L1 might be decidable or undecidable. Reducibility guarantees that a decider for L2 would yield a decider for L1, but the converse (L2 undecidable implies L1 undecidable) need not hold. Provide examples: the empty language (decidable) can reduce to an undecidable L2, and taking L1 = L2 gives an undecidable L1.

This is incorrect. L1 does not have to be decidable just because it reduces to an undecidable L2. Reducibility only implies that if L2 were decidable then L1 would be decidable; it does not imply the reverse. Provide counterexamples: L1 can be decidable (e.g., the empty language) or undecidable (e.g., L1 = L2).

title: Given some languages &ClosureProperties

text: Given some languages
solution:
Key facts:

  • L1 is REC (decidable).

  • L2 is RE but not REC, so the complement of L2 is not decidable.

Assume for contradiction that the complement of L2 is polynomial-time reducible to L1.

  1. Then there is a polynomial-time computable function f such that x is in the complement of L2 exactly when f(x) is in L1.

  2. Because L1 is decidable, we can decide membership in the complement of L2 by computing f(x) and running the decider for L1 on f(x).

  3. Hence the complement of L2 would be decidable, contradicting the given that L2 is RE but not decidable.

Conclusion: The reduction cannot exist, so the correct answer is that such a reduction is not possible.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. If the complement of the RE-but-not-decidable language is reducible to a decidable language, then the complement would be decidable: compute the reduction and run the decider for the decidable language. That would make the complement decidable, contradicting the given that the original language is RE but not decidable. Therefore the reduction cannot exist.

This states that the complement of the RE-but-not-decidable language would become decidable if the reduction held. While that follows from the reduction plus a decider for the decidable language, it leads to a contradiction with the given property that the original language is RE but not decidable. Therefore the assumed reduction cannot hold, so this consequence cannot actually happen in the given setting.

Incorrect. The reducibility assumption does not change the decidability status of the target language. The language given as decidable remains decidable; you cannot make a decidable language become undecidable by a reduction from another language.

Incorrect. The target language is given as decidable (REC), so it is already semi-decidable (RE) as well; reducibility from another language does not transform a decidable language into merely semi-decidable. The statement is not the right consequence of the reduction assumption.

title: Which of the following statements are True? &ClosureProperties
subject: Theory of Computation
text: Which of the following statements are True?

options.html: Equivalence of two or more CFG whose language is DCFL is decidable.
Equivalence of two or more regular grammars is semi-decidable.
We can't reduce P1 ≤P P2 in polynomial time if P1 is not RE and P2 is REC.

solution:
Statement: Equivalence of two or more CFG whose language is DCFL is decidable.

Verdict: True.

Reason: Deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs), which are the languages recognized by deterministic pushdown automata (DPDAs), have decidable equivalence. L. Sénizergues (1997) proved decidability of equivalence for deterministic pushdown automata. For students: determinism restricts the class enough to allow an algorithm deciding equivalence, unlike the general context-free case where equivalence is undecidable.

Statement: Equivalence of two or more regular grammars is semi-decidable.

Verdict: False.

Reason: Equivalence of regular grammars (regular languages) is decidable. A standard method is to convert each grammar to a deterministic finite automaton (DFA), build the product automaton for the symmetric difference of the two DFAs, and check whether that product accepts any string (emptiness). Alternatively, minimize both DFAs and compare them. These procedures always halt, so equivalence is decidable.

Statement: We can't reduce P1 to P2 in polynomial time if P1 is not RE and P2 is REC.

Verdict: True.

Reason: A polynomial-time many-one reduction is a special case of a computable function f with the property that x is in P1 iff f(x) is in P2. If P2 is recursive (decidable), then computing f(x) and deciding membership of f(x) in P2 yields a decision procedure for P1, which would make P1 decidable (hence recursively enumerable). This contradicts the assumption that P1 is not even recursively enumerable, so no such polynomial-time reduction can exist.

Statement: L = {<TM> | TM accepts ε} is undecidable.

Verdict: True.

Reason: Reduce from the general acceptance problem. Given any Turing machine M and input w, construct a machine M' that on input ε simulates M on w and accepts iff M accepts w, and on any other input behaves (for example) by rejecting immediately. Then M' accepts ε exactly when M accepts w. If we could decide membership in {<TM> | TM accepts ε} we would decide the general acceptance problem, which is undecidable. Therefore the language is undecidable.

Correct statements (exact text):

  • Equivalence of two or more CFG whose language is DCFL is decidable.

  • We can't reduce P1 to P2 in polynomial time if P1 is not RE and P2 is REC.

  • L = {<TM> | TM accepts ε} is undecidable.

optionFeedback.html: True. Equivalence of two grammars whose languages are deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs) is decidable. Sénizergues (1997) proved decidability of equivalence for deterministic pushdown automata (DPDAs); since DCFLs are exactly the languages recognized by DPDAs, this yields decidability for equivalence of such grammars. Note that this result relies on determinism — equivalence for general context-free grammars is undecidable.

False. Equivalence of regular grammars (regular languages) is decidable, not merely semi-decidable. A standard procedure is: convert each grammar to a DFA, construct the DFA for the symmetric difference (via the product construction), and check whether that DFA accepts any string (emptiness). Alternatively, minimize both DFAs and check whether they are isomorphic. These algorithms always halt, so equivalence for regular languages is decidable.

True. If there were a polynomial-time (or any computable many-one) reduction f from a language P1 that is not even recursively enumerable (not RE) to a recursive (decidable) language P2, then to decide membership in P1 you would compute f(x) and decide membership of f(x) in P2 (which is decidable). That would make P1 decidable (hence RE), contradicting that P1 is not RE. Therefore no such polynomial-time reduction can exist.

True. The language of encodings of Turing machines that accept the empty string, {<TM> | TM accepts ε}, is undecidable. A simple reduction shows this: given a TM M and input w, build a TM M' that on input ε simulates M on input w and accepts iff M accepts w. Then M' accepts ε iff M accepts w, so deciding acceptance of ε would decide the general acceptance problem, which is undecidable.

• P (Polynomial time): The class of decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine (a standard computer) in polynomial time. Examples include sorting a list or finding the shortest path in a graph.

  • NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial time): The class of decision problems for which a given candidate solution can be verified by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.

If a problem is in P, we can solve it quickly from scratch. If we can solve it quickly, we can also verify a proposed solution quickly just by running our fast algorithm and checking if the answer matches. Therefore, every problem that is efficiently solvable (P) is also efficiently verifiable (NP).

title: Which of the following statements are TRUE The problem of
subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Which of the following statements are TRUE?

  1. The problem of determining whether there exists a cycle in an undirected graph is in P.

  2. The problem of determining whether there exists a cycle in an undirected graph is in NP.

  3. If a problem A is NP-Complete, there exists a non-deterministic polynomial time algorithm to solve A.
solution:
Concept

Two complexity facts govern this problem. First, the inclusion P ⊆ NP always holds: any decision problem solvable by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is also solvable by a non-deterministic one (the machine simply never uses its guessing power), so membership in P implies membership in NP. Second, by definition NP is exactly the class of decision problems for which a non-deterministic Turing machine runs in polynomial time, and every NP-Complete problem lies inside NP — so an NP-Complete problem necessarily has a non-deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Applying it to each statement

  1. “Undirected-graph cycle detection is in P.” A single depth-first search (or a union-find pass over the edges) detects a cycle in O(V + E) time — a deterministic polynomial-time procedure. Hence the problem is in P. TRUE.

  2. “The same problem is in NP.” Since it is in P and P ⊆ NP, it is automatically in NP (a verifier can also be built in polynomial time). TRUE.

  3. “An NP-Complete problem A has a non-deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.” Every NP-Complete problem is, by definition, a member of NP, and NP is precisely the set of problems decidable by a non-deterministic polynomial-time machine. So such an algorithm exists. TRUE.

Cross-check

All three statements hold, so the true set is exactly {1, 2, 3}. A common trap is to think NP means “hard / not in P”; in fact P ⊆ NP, so a polynomial problem being in NP is not a contradiction, and “non-deterministic polynomial time” is simply the defining property of NP, not a claim about tractability.

optionFeedback.html: Reaching this requires checking each membership claim against its own definition — the cost of cycle detection on an undirected graph, the containment relationship between the classes P and NP, and the defining property of NP that every NP-Complete problem must satisfy. Verify each independently rather than pattern-matching the combination.

This selection rests on a judgement about whether an NP-Complete problem must admit a non-deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The decisive test is the formal definition of NP and what membership in it requires of NP-Complete problems; settle that statement strictly from the definition rather than from intuition about difficulty.

This selection rests on a judgement about the running time of deciding whether an undirected graph contains a cycle. The decisive test is whether a single linear-time graph traversal suffices; settle that statement from the actual algorithm rather than from a general assumption that graph problems are costly.

This selection rests on a judgement about whether a problem already solvable in polynomial time also qualifies as a member of NP. The decisive test is the containment relationship between the classes P and NP; settle that statement from that relationship rather than from an assumption that NP excludes easy problems.
